#864. The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters â "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing â injury aside â that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

"Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow."

A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

So far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

Even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he says.

Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," says 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football."

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" â champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

"I want to get away from this east-west debate," says Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR."

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

"The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a plan, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act."

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition."

Borussia Dortmund president â and Bundesliga chairman â Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option."

Support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion."

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model â but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote announced two key changes:

Suddenly, the four new leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future."

The Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that."

For Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe â completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

This season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

And before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!"

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) announced the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

"[The issue] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent."

Any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season â too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

"You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he says before heading out for training.

"It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted."

#863. Mustaki out of World Cup play-off with knee injury

Chloe Mustaki is a key figure for Carla Ward's Republic of Ireland side

Republic of Ireland defender Chloe Mustaki has been forced to withdraw from her side's 2027 Women's World Cup play-off final against Poland next month after rupturing her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

The 31-year-old sustained the injury in action for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool in the League Cup last week.

Her club have confirmed the centre-back will miss the rest of the season and that their medical team will "determine the best course of action for her rehabilitation and recovery".

Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward said she was "absolutely devastated" for the player who will be a huge loss in the side's efforts to make it the tournament in Brazil next summer.

She added: "It is a huge blow for the entire squad because of how important she is to this group, both on the pitch with her consistency and leadership, and off the pitch with the incredible character and positivity she brings to the dressing room.

"This is a really difficult setback, but Chloe is loved by us all. Everyone in the squad, the staff and the association is fully behind her, and we will give her all the love and support she needs to make a full recovery."

Ward will not call up a replacement to her squad with the 24-player panel set to gather in Dublin on Tuesday.

They will play the first leg of the play-off in Gdansk on 1 December with the return fixture at the Aviva Stadium four days later. Both games kick off at 17:00 GMT.

#862. Norwich hit back to hold QPR

Norwich City vs Queens Park Rangers. EFL Championship.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Norwich City and Queens Park Rangers at Carrow Road on Tuesday night; Canaries draw their first game of the season as Anthony Musaba cancels out Harvey Vale’s opener.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Norwich's impressive run of victories came to an end as QPR held them to a 1-1 draw at Carrow Road.

The Canaries had won their previous five Championship fixtures but had to come from behind to pick up a point this time around after Harvey Vale had fired the visitors in front just before the break.

Philippe Clement's side were quickly back on level terms in the second half through a well-taken Anthony Musaba effort, but were well contained after that as Rangers registered a well-deserved point.

After a slow start, the match burst into life with a flurry of activity around the mid-point of the first half.

Norwich thought they had taken the lead on 19 minutes when Harry Darling got a touch on an in-swinging Jacob Wright free-kick but the effort was ruled out for offside.

Andre Brooks then saw a low shot from the edge of the area come back off the upright, while at the other end Dan Grimshaw did well to palm away a goal-bound effort from Vale.

Rangers were giving the hosts plenty to think about and took the lead four minutes before the break when Vale made another opportunity count.

Wolverhampton Wanderers 3-0 Derby County: Adam Armstrong nets twice in Wolves win

Charlton Athletic 4-0 Lincoln City: Addicks sweep to victory at The Valley

Cardiff City 0-4 Preston North End: Graham Alexander's side romp to victory

Bristol City 1-1 Wrexham: Cameron Pring earns point for Robins

Sheffield United 1-1 Southampton: Sydie Peck strikes again to earn point for Blades

Portsmouth 1-0 West Ham United: Scott Parker stays winless as Odin Bailey nets Pompey winner

The Republic of Ireland international had plenty to do after latching on to Kealey Adamson's pass but despite having Ruairi McConville and Darling in close attendance, he worked himself some space in the area before firing a powerful shot past Grimshaw.

Norwich were back on level terms within three minutes of the restart after a poor clearance by goalkeeper Pierce Charles was punished. It went straight to Musaba, who played a quick one-two with Mathias Kvistgaarden before confidently finding the roof of the net.

Vale fired inches wide as Rangers sought a quick response while substitute Oscar Schwartau was foiled by a good save from Charles as the game entered its final 10 minutes.

Norwich continued to press for a winner but could find no way through as they drew a game for the first time this season.

"This team will never settle for a draw - they will always keep going for the win but in football it doesn't always happen.

"After going behind we showed the right mentality, got our goal and kept pushing them back, with the fans playing their part, but unfortunately we couldn't get the second goal we deserved.

"We were up against a well-organised side and knew it was going to be tough but I thought the momentum was with us in the first half too and we just needed a bit of luck.

"We had a goal ruled out through a very tight offside decision and then Andre (Brooks) hit the post.

"When we went behind it became an even tougher task because we know how difficult they are to break down but our response was really good with everyone playing their part, including the lads who came off the bench."

"That's four points from two very tough away games, Millwall and Norwich, which is a very positive outcome and all credit to the players for that.

"We were up against a side who had won their previous five games, scoring 17 goals, and it was a very good performance, with a draw a fair result I feel.

"We started very well, both with and without the ball, playing with a good tempo, and scored a very good goal.

"Obviously we were disappointed to concede so early in the second half but the lads showed great character to stick to the game plan. They defended properly as a team and we also had some chances.

"I am lucky to have a special group of players here and although they are a young group I thought they showed great maturity out there to come away with a deserved point."

Arsenal wonderkid Ethan Nwaneri hasn't established himself on loan - and now faces further competition for his place

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ethan Nwaneri's Arsenal career appears to be floundering, with the on-loan Borussia Dortmund teenager facing a further transfer setback.

Nwaneri returns to his parent club tonight in the Champions League with the Bundesliga giants and is eligible to face Arsenal despite still being owned by the Gunners.

But beyond this campaign, his future remains uncertain, with manager Mikel Arteta even recently alluding to the teenager's struggles at Signal Iduna Park.

Nwaneri became the Premier League's youngest-ever player in 2022 at the age of 15 – with Max Dowman later taking that record – before establishing himself in the 2024/25 season as a serious option on the right wing for the Gunners.

But after going out on loan at Marseille last term and heading to Dortmund this time, the teenager is yet to impress, with Arteta even admitting this week that “moments are not enough” for Nwaneri in his development and that consistency must follow.

A report from Sport Witness, likewise, reads as bad news for the 19-year-old, with the Gunners now pursuing a move for Gilberto Mora as soon as January.

Mora was the youngest player selected for the 2026 World Cup and has impressed hugely in his native Mexico, courting the attention of virtually every big club in Europe.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In attacking midfield areas, Arsenal already have the likes of Martin Odegaard, Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Max Dowman – with the latter two options on the wing – and should Arsenal bring in another teenage talent, Nwaneri's first-team opportunities would appear even scarcer.

FourFourTwo understands that the Gunners were open to offers for the starlet over the summer, opting to retain him and develop him at one of the best finishing schools in European football, though the paths of Nwaneri and Hale End colleague Myles Lewis-Skelly have been drastically different, thanks, in part, due to competition for places.

With Liverpool also circling for Mora, however, the Gunners may well have to present a particularly enticing package to secure the 18-year-old.

According to the report, the youngster has a release clause of around €25 million, making any move for him particularly costly – and suggesting that the Gunners could well incorporate him into their first team immediately.

Nwaneri, meanwhile, is valued by Transfermarkt at €25m. Arsenal return to Champions League action tonight against Dortmund at the Emirates Stadium.

#860. European shares join a global sell-off as AI spending fears rattle Wall Street and Asian markets

European shares have fallen after sharp losses in Asia and on Wall Street. Doubts over huge AI investments and fears of curbs following the Democrats' US midterm victory have rattled global markets.

European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.

European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.

Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US markets were hammered on Thursday by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.

The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending plans and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.

The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.

"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

"Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that shows up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in."

#859. IFA 'positive' over upgrades needed for World Cup

Windsor Park would require 5,000 additional seats to host games at the 2035 World Cup

The Irish Football Association's director of women's football Angela Platt said the organisation is "still working through" plans with the Northern Ireland government to ensure there is funding available to make the necessary upgrades to Windsor Park in time for the 2035 World Cup.

It was confirmed on Monday that Northern Ireland, England, Scotland and Wales, the only bidders for the tournament in nine years' time, had been ratified as co-hosts.

Of the 19 venues proposed by the 'All Together' bid, Belfast's Windsor Park is the sole stadium in Northern Ireland, but would require an additional 5,000 seats to its current capacity of 18,500 as well as changes to the pitch and floodlights.

"We're obviously working with our government partners who've committed their support to help us do that, and we'll continue our endeavours to make sure that we work towards that," Platt told BBC NI's Stephen Watson.

"We know that the Northern Ireland Executive has given a commitment to back us and do whatever they can to support us in our endeavours to make sure we're ready for that hosting of the Women's World Cup in 2035.

"We have a few years to make sure we work through that."

Northern Ireland was involved in a similar bid to host games at Euro 2028, but plans for fixtures in Belfast at that tournament fell through when the government said it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in the required timescale.

Platt said that "was in the past" and that the organisation were focused on the work required to avoid any repeat.

"We're still working towards making sure that it does happen and we're positive. We know that the work is there to make sure that it happens," she added.

"It's obviously disappointing when something that people work so hard to put together doesn't come to fruition, but certainly that's in the past for us.

"From our perspective, working for women's football, this is a great opportunity for Northern Ireland to get behind this and actually make sure that we do everything we can to host our Women's World Cup games here."

UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms

Plans to increase Windsor Park capacity to 23,750

There is no guarantee that, even as co-hosts, there would an automatic qualification spot for Northern Ireland.

The side last qualified for a major tournament at Euro 2022 and Platt believes bringing the World Cup to the country has the potential to "inspire a new generation".

"I think it can have a huge impact. We've always been blessed that we have had our women's team involved in the Women's Euros in 2022, and through my role, I get to visit other nations hosting tournaments such as this," she said.

"I was in Sydney for the Women's World Cup (2023) and obviously saw the impact hosting a tournament like that had in New Zealand and Australia, and likewise for the Euros in England and Switzerland recently.

"That impact is significant. It's the growth of the game, it's the engagement, it's the legacy. So much positivity can come out of hosting major tournaments and we're excited to play our part in this and it can only have benefits for Northern Ireland in general."

#857. 'Our Super Bowl moment' - what can WSL learn from booming US league?

Kansas City Current, who were formed in 2020, won this year's National Women's Soccer League championship

"It's turning into our Super Bowl moment."

Sarah Jones Simmer, chief operating officer of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), could not wait for the championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current on Saturday night.

The NWSL showpiece was played out in front of a sellout crowd of more than 19,000 at Audi Field in Washington DC, with tickets retailing at more than $300 (Â£229).

Ultimately, the Current triumphed 2-1 to clinch their first title, condemning Spirit to an unwanted record of three lost finals in a row.

Just a few hours earlier on this side of the Atlantic, Alexia Putellas, who last month was crowned the best player in the world for the third time at the Ballon d'Or ceremony, was scoring twice for London City against Crystal Palace in front of 4,000 people in Bromley.

It is a totally unfair comparison. After all, a championship final is the type of jamboree the USA does particularly well.

Nevertheless, women's football is booming in America at the moment, with attendance figures at record highs, more franchises joining the league and club retail sales double those of 2025.

So what is behind the explosion in popularity?

And what can the Women's Super League learn from it?

The US is the most successful nation in women's international football.

The four-time World Cup winners (1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019) and five-time Olympic gold medallists, the nation of Mia Hamm, Alex Morgan and Megan Rapinoe, has a history of winning - and the domestic game is key.

"If anything, soccer is more seen as a women's sport [in the USA]," says broadcaster Jacqui Oatley, who currently commentates on the NWSL for ESPN.

"Women have won World Cups and Olympic Games - and the men have been nowhere near as successful."

While teams in the United States became professional in 2001 - for WSL teams it was 2018 - the top flight has taken several different guises over the years.

The current NWSL kicked off in 2013 as an eight-team competition, and has since expanded to 16 franchises, with two more joining from 2028.

There is no relegation and Kansas City's victory on Saturday means the league has had eight different winners since its iteration.

As the below graph shows, the ownership picture for these sides is far more varied than in the UK, with American sides much less dependent on their male counterparts.

Indeed, Kansas City are blazing a trail. Established in December 2020, unaffiliated to a men's side and backed by ambitious owners that include Brittany Mahomes - the wife of NFL quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

Winning the championship is the crowning achievement for an ambitious franchise and such success is something independent London City hope to emulate in the UK. They are four points from the WSL summit nearly halfway through the 2026-27 season.

Kansas City were also the first club to build a bespoke stadium solely for women's football and the demand for seats at their 11,500-seater CPKC Stadium is huge. Earlier this year, Brighton announced their own purpose-built venue, planned for 2030-31.

"I think our independence is a hallmark of the league," says the NWSL's Jones Simmer.

"It is something we are very proud of. It allows us to invest in our own growth, prioritise the women's game and ensure resources are flowing to it."

It is markedly different from the UK set-up, where all WSL teams bar London City are, at least, affiliated and more often financially reliant on the men's side.

But that presents just as much of an opportunity, according to Jones Simmer.

"I know Nikki [Doucet, chief executive of the WSL] and I admire what she is building," she says.

"There's a really unique opportunity to build on the legacy of these 100-year-old men's clubs that are household names, to build women's brands that embrace the legacy but also have their own identity."

Bespoke women's football stadiums? Why US sides are making the move

Brighton plan Europe's first purpose-built Â£80m women's stadium

Washington Spirit's Trinity Rodman benefited from a NWSL decision in December 2025 to lift the league's salary cap for a 'High Impact Player'

Fans of both the NWSL and the WSL are spoiled when it comes to talent.

Most of the US national team play their club football at home, with the likes of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Rose Lavelle household names.

International stars such as Malawi's Temwa Chawinga at Kansas City, who came 10th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings, and former Chelsea striker Sam Kerr further enhance the league's quality.

"Where it starts is the product on the pitch," says Jones Simmer. "The quality of football has to be incredible and we have the best players in the world.

"And they are incredibly engaging with our fans. For so many supporters, their entry point to the league is they care about a particular player."

Provided the standard of competition is present, Jones Simmer says fans will return - and her confidence is backed up by the numbers.

In 2026, the average gate for an NWSL match has been more than 11,000 - only Arsenal in the WSL consistently receive a higher attendance than that, albeit the US is almost five times more populous than the UK.

On Thursday, the final few tickets for the NWSL's showpiece were retailing at $300 on ticket site Viagogo, with Jones Simmer suggesting resale tickets could be purchased at six times market value in advance of the match.

As London City and Washington Spirit owner Michele Kang put it: "The answer could not be clearer that there is an audience for the women's game."

"It's our job to hook fans by making sure they have a great experience watching a game in a venue and that's about the quality of the product," Jones Simmer adds.

"Once folks have that experience, it's a really easy yes to tune in again."

Families v loyal fans - women's football's attendance dilemma

Not that quality is an issue in the WSL where high-class footballers abound. Take Putellas, goal machine Khadija Shaw and most of England's double European Championship-winning squad for example.

American stars such as Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma at Chelsea, and Manchester City's Sam Coffey, have also swapped the US for the WSL in the past two years.

Broadcaster Oatley, who has been covering women's football since the 2005 World Cup, is keen for such players to be more visible off the pitch.

"I would love to see WSL players on mainstream TV shows, podcasts, social media platforms, not just on women's football programmes where the audience already knows everything about them," she says.

"It would not be for everyone, but for those who are comfortable, who have the biggest personalities, I think we could use that much more to grow our audience."

Oatley has been covering NWSL games for the past four seasons and she believes US clubs have mastered putting on events.

"When you're trying to promote a product in sport, you can't guarantee the team is going to play well and win," she says.

"But you can ensure the people who come to the game have a great experience.

"I love the enthusiasm, the positivity, the vibe of 'let's make this big'. It's a brilliant experience."

It is a balance the WSL wrestles with. With attendances plateauing this season, questions have arisen around its target audience and whether to market matches such as the north London derby between Tottenham and Arsenal as a rivalry or a family-friendly event.

Oatley's perspective is that it ought to be both, while recognising the different challenges in this country.

"I didn't understand that criticism," she says, "because they weren't saying: 'Only come to this game if you're a family'. It was being promoted all round.

"I don't think it's one size fits all marketing wise - the main thing is awareness."

The NWSL Fan Fest at The Wharf in Washington DC was part of a series of events around the championship game on Saturday

It is a challenge the NWSL has embraced, and seen attendances rise accordingly.

"We want to ensure that we provided a big enough tent where everyone can feel welcome and included, whether they're there for the rivalries and the competitive tactics, or they're experiencing it for the first time," says Jones Simmer.

"To grow the sport, all fans need to be able to come to an NWSL game and have a great experience."

This season, league finalists Current and Spirit played at a remarkable 17 different times between them, reflecting the four timezones and vast nature of the USA.

It is all part of the country's sporting landscape, but given the WSL's continued conundrum about fixture scheduling, it is interesting that NWSL supporters manage to find the matches regardless.

"I have a lot of sympathy with schedulers because men's football got there first," Oatley says.

"Maybe the solution is deciding certain time slots are for women's football and sticking with them."

It does not appear the growth in the NWSL will slow down any time soon.

The Women's World Cup in Brazil next summer will feature the USA as one of the favourites and women's soccer will feature at the Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028.

The US will also host the 2031 Women's World Cup.

"It is amazing how the NWSL is cracking into culture," Jones Simmer says.

"We get excited about these catalytic opportunities to expand the community engagement, awareness and relevance of the NWSL."

#855. Andreatta's masterplan to shock Sweden & take Scots to World Cup

Scotland women play Sweden in Paisley next Tuesday, with the second leg in Stockholm on 5 December

Scotland intend to bring fancied Sweden's World Cup dream "crashing down - and do it in a truly Scottish way", according to women's head coach Melissa Andreatta.

Scotland face a two-legged World Cup qualifying play-off against powerhouses Sweden, who are managed by Andreatta's former boss Tony Gustavsson.

The Swedes, who have been semi-finalists at the two previous Women's World Cups and are ranked eighth in the world, will be strong favourites to reach the tournament in Brazil next summer.

Andreatta, who has eight wins, two losses and four draws from her 14 games in charge of Scotland, was Gustavsson's deputy when he was Australia head coach from 2020 to 2024.

While the two have a connection from those years, the Australian is very much in business mode with next week's first leg at St Mirren Park looming.

"A few weeks ago Tony reached out, sent me a few messages and I took my time to respond," she told BBC Scotland.

"It wasn't much about football, just connecting on a personal level - which is probably a good thing, because I can be quite competitive. I just want to focus on business and not the personal level.

"I'm sure, like he is, all we're focused on is how we're going to win."

Listen to the full interview with Melissa Andreatta

The Scots finished top of their qualifying group earlier this year after four wins from their six games before beating the Czech Republic 5-2 on aggregate in the play-off semi-final.

That set up the exacting play-off final against the Swedes, a team who narrowly missed out on a spot in the final at the previous two World Cups.

Scotland have made just one appearance at the tournament, in 2019, and Andreatta is excited by the prospect of getting one over her old boss for her new home.

"It's going to be a great occasion to face them at home first," she added.

"They are such a powerhouse nation that carries so much expectation to go to their next tournament. We want to bring that all crashing down and do that in a truly Scottish way. That's what we're going to focus on.

"I definitely won't be looking at their dug out, I'll be focused on us and what we need to do to get the result and go to another tournament.

"They are an exceptional team but we won't be swayed by a team's reputation or ranking.

"We firmly believe that anything is possible. Once that whistle goes, if you've done the work and you're prepared you're in the position to make anything happen. With this group of players and staff I know that's possible, we can take it to anyone on any given day.

"It is a massive challenge but we love those moments and that's why we're here. We've earned it."

Melissa Andreatta with daughter Mackenzie after Scotland beat the Czech Republic in their World Cup qualification semi-final

There are more than 10,000 miles between Brisbane - where Andreatta grew up - and Ayr in Scotland, where she now calls home.

While the climate may be vastly different, there's one thing they do have in common - the beach.

"I love the coastal life. In Australia it's a big part of your lifestyle, being outdoors. I think there's something about the sea, being near it. Relaxing, calming, balancing," she said.

It has been 18 months since Andreatta was announced as Pedro Martinez Losa's successor as manager of the Scotland women's team and now, with her family alongside her - including two-year-old daughter Mackenzie - she feels at home.

"We've definitely settled in," she added. "We have the spots that we go to, our routine, we love it here. It's been a great landing spot for us on such a big move."

But what does her daughter make of her mum's job?

"She's got no idea," says Andreatta. "She just think's mum's on TV. Whenever she sees me she gets excited. Having her at the games is super special, being able to hold her on the pitch. She's such a joy.

"You do these things to make people proud and I want to make her proud."

Andreatta has made a promising start as Scotland manager - but now faces a huge task

Scotland without captain Weir for World Cup play-off

New strategy launched to transform Scottish women's football over 10 years

Andreatta was sitting in the pubs of Scotland over the summer as the Tartan Army headed over to the United States in their droves to watch the men's team compete at a first World Cup in almost 30 years.

The women won't have to wait that long if they can book a spot on the plane to Brazil next summer.

Andreatta is hoping to see just as many kilts on the Copacabana beach as there were in the bars of Boston.

"There is a strong desire among the group, not only players but also the staff, there is this desire to make their nation proud and show Scotland that the women's national team belongs here and deserves as much of the limelight as the men's," she added.

"Together we can make our nation proud and what better way to do it? To have our men at the World Cup and then the following summer our women.

"Watching from afar, what the fans did over there and in Boston, why can't we do that in Rio? That's what I'm envisaging but there's a lot to do and achieve before we get there."

#853. Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

Evidence suggests exercise can keep more cancer patients alive. But what does "living longer" actually mean, and who does it apply to?

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.   In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.

#852. Cherki salvages draw with Napoli but Man City frustrate

Manchester City vs Napoli. UEFA Champions League Round 1.

Etihad StadiumAttendance: Attendance48,076.

Match report as Manchester City drew 2-2 with Napoli in the Champions League at the Etihad Stadium. Rasmus Hojlund and Noa Lang twice put the Italian side in front but equalisers from Ayyoub Bouaddi and Rayan Cherki earned Enzo Maresca's men a point

Football Features Writer @ghostgoal

Rayan Cherki’s late strike salvaged a 2-2 draw for Manchester City at home to Napoli in the Champions League but Enzo Maresca’s side again struggled to find their fluency.

Former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund opened the scoring for the Italian side and though Ayyoub Bouaddi equalised, Noa Lang's volley stunned the Etihad Stadium as Napoli restored their lead late on. Cherki's goal at least secured a point.

The draw leaves City in sixth spot in the Champions League table but they are likely to drop out of the top eight by Wednesday evening and have now gone 10 games without a clean sheet. Maresca's men look vulnerable ahead of the trip to Arsenal on Sunday.

With little to cheer in the first half, the home crowd took most pleasure in serenading Kevin De Bruyne on his return - King Kev declared one banner - and he gave glimpses of his quality, twice cutting City's defence apart. But the sluggish tempo suited a veteran.

It was all a little too slow from City. Maresca was trying to tighten up in midfield, picking Bouaddi as well as Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez for only the second time. But it left this City side short of thrust in the last third despite Allan's impressive endeavour.

It needed a strong save from Gianluigi Donnarumma to ensure City went in level at the break. Sam Beukema made firm contact with a free header inside the box but the Napoli defender placed it too close to the goalkeeper. The home side did not heed the warning.

Billy Gilmour fed Hojlund inside the box on the angle and he got the shot away under pressure from Marc Guehi to beat Donnarumma low to his left. It was a sweet moment for the Danish striker, 23, whose United links had seen him booed by the City fans.

Arsenal vs Borussia Dortmund: Gunners player ratings from Champions League draw at Emirates

Hibernian 2-1 Dundee | Scottish Premiership Highlights

Arsenal and Manchester City's problems analysed as both set to meet in bumper Premier League clash this weekend

Erling Haaland frustrated with Manchester City form: 'When you don't win, you question everything'

Enzo Maresca satisfied with Manchester City's performance vs Napoli in the Champions League

Chelsea transfer news: Blues will push to sign Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott in January - Paper Talk

But Napoli's lead did not last long thanks to Bouaddi. The elegant Moroccan midfielder had yet to score a goal at senior level in his career but his left-footed effort found its way through Vanja Milinkovic-Savic. Substitute Jeremy Doku provided the spark required.

City were pushing for a winner at that stage, but Lang's exquisite volley on the counter-attack was a reminder that Maresca is having trouble controlling counter-attacks. At least he had kept the mercurial Cherki on the pitch to help avoid a damaging defeat.

But after that seven-game winning run in the Premier League, it is one point from four domestically and now this unconvincing effort in front of their own supporters. City are still a work in progress under Maresca. They will need to improve plenty at Arsenal.

The game ended amid confusion when the referee blew the final whistle with the big screen showing around 20 seconds of the two minutes of added time still to play. City were in possession and moving the ball up the pitch. Donnarumma was among those incensed at the decision as City players surrounded the official who responded by pointing to his watch. The problem is that this watch must have been telling a different time to the one everyone else was seeing.

55 - GOAL! Hojlund fired in the opener for Napoli

67 - GOAL! Bouaddi's strike levelled it for Man City

76 - GOAL! Lang volleyed in to restore Napoli's lead

86 - GOAL! Cherki's low strike salvaged a point

Man City captain Erling Haaland speaking to TNT Sports:

"We tried to push but we couldn't. It's not good enough. We let them in too easily and were unable to control or attack the game as we want.

"Football can be so difficult and easy. When you win games everything is easy and you know exactly what to do, when you don't win you start to question everything. The perfect thing would be to don't think but it's difficult in these moments.

"We have so much quality. It's about getting that quality out of every single player. We have to regroup to stay positive and bring the energy on the pitch.

"We go to the champions next. The most difficult game of the season. We need a top, top performance."

#851. Can returning Beattie and Haughey make an impact?

Beattie won the last of her 13 caps last year while the uncapped Haughey was last called into the senior squad in 2021

Michael McArdle has decided the upcoming friendly double-header against Greece is the perfect time to bring back Kerry Beattie and Ella Haughey from the international wilderness.

Glentoran midfielder Chloe McCarron is also in under McArdle for the first time after a lengthily absence, but the Glentoran midfielder would likely have been included sooner if not for a spell on the sidelines through injury.

Beattie won her last cap a year ago while Haughey will hope to make a senior debut in one of the two games against Greece at Inver Park after she was an unused substitute in friendlies against England and Scotland in her sole call up in 2021.

The inclusion of both players, who have been in good form at their clubs, shows McArdle is willing to keep the door open for a return to the international squad if players are performing at club level.

Magill returns to NI squad for Greece friendlies

Portsmouth striker Beattie has been in and out of squads since her debut in 2021.

The 24-year-old has four goals in 13 caps, the last of which she won against Iceland in the Nations League play-off a year ago.

A prolific forward during two spells at Glentoran, she has struggled for consistency in moves across to Scotland with the likes of Glasgow City, Hearts and Aberdeen.

She left the Dons in the summer and consulted with McArdle when deciding upon her next move, before joining WSL 2 side Portsmouth.

Beattie has eight goals in all competitions for a Pompey side languishing at the bottom of the table and McArdle is pleased she has settled in well.

"Kerry had spells at Hearts and Aberdeen and for whatever reason it didn't quite work out at both, she had good spells but not a consistent run to express herself," McArdle said.

"The move to Portsmouth, I was delighted she reached out to me for some advice, it's an alignment for her and it's been a great move on and off the pitch. It's allowed her to enjoy herself but also play 90 minutes and be that focal point striker.

"She will have been disappointed not to make the squad for the [World Cup] play-off [against Portugal] with her form but she worked hard and she's back in, I'm delighted for her."

Beattie faces stiff competition for the starting striker role from the likes of returning captain Simone Magill and Kess Elmore, who impressed in the last camp and scored against Portugal, but she should receive some minutes across the two games and will be keen to grasp her chance to make an impact.

Left-back Haughey was called up to the senior squad as a 16-year-old under Kenny Shiels, but did not feature

West Brom defender Haughey's last involvement with NI came when she represented the under-19s in 2023.

A Lisburn Rangers player when Kenny Shiels included her in the senior squad as a 16-year-old, Haughey then moved to Nottingham Forest before settling at the Baggies, who play in the National League.

The left-back, 22, has been a regular this season for the club in the third tier and combines playing with her university studies.

Left-back has been a problem position for NI which McArdle has been trying to address as demonstrated by him bringing in Lucy-Jayne Grant in the last camp and Haughey for this window to allow Rebecca Holloway to play as a central defender.

Haughey will be competing with Grant to fill that full-back role on the left side and McArdle believes she is more than capable of doing so having tried to bring her back into the squad earlier in his reign.

"Ella's been at West Brom for a few years now. She has real potential, strong, athletic potential. We tried to call her up sooner but there were some challenges," he explained.

"She's probably been one of their top performers and one of the top performers in the league. Delighted she's earned this opportunity and hopefully she can make her debut and achieve her first cap."

McArdle has made a concerted to continue to widen the player pool available to him as he aims to build depth ahead of the Nations League campaign next year, but if Beattie and Haughey catch the eye it will show that giving chances to those previously involved under different managers could be another possibility.

Are the Premier League’s London clubs at an advantage? Arsenal prepare to put that unique theory to the test

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Having made their longest Premier League away trip of the season to Newcastle last week, Arsenal can settle into familiar surroundings for the festive period: the Gunners don’t leave London again until mid-January when they travel to Hull.

Between now and then, Arsenal’s longest away day takes them just 22 kilometres to Brentford - Google Maps says the average person could walk from the Emirates to the Gtech in under four hours, never mind a professional footballer.

That’s the third of 11 straight games in the capital for the Gunners, which will become 12 if they’re drawn at home in the third round of the FA Cup, beginning with Tuesday’s Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund. Recent history suggests an interesting theory about such home comforts.

Eleven games into their title defence, Arsenal sit second in the Premier League away table with four wins, one draw and one defeat from six games on the road. Not that it’s anything new for the Gunners to occupy such heights: they’ve boasted the top flight’s best away record in each of the last four seasons.

And that comes with the territory of being a London club. Across the last 10 Premier League campaigns not impacted by pandemic crowd restrictions (so excluding 2019/20 and 2020/21), only once have more clubs from London had a bottom-half away record than a top-half away record. That was last term, when four of the seven London clubs finished in the bottom 10 of the away table (Crystal Palace, Brentford, Fulham and West Ham).

In each of the other nine seasons in question, at least 57 per cent of the Premier League’s London clubs have finished with one of the best 10 away records in the division; in 2016/17, all five of them did (Chelsea, Tottenham, Arsenal, Palace and West Ham).

So, is it an advantage to be a London club?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There’s not really a simple answer to that question (sorry), but we can still pull together some interesting takeaways.

This season, the average Premier League club will travel 153 kilometres for an away fixture. For two clubs, that average climbs to over 300km: the league’s two most north-easterly sides, Sunderland (350km) and Newcastle (347km), and the most south-westerly, Bournemouth (317km). Conversely, one side will travel a touch under 200km on average: Coventry (198km) – in that sense, you might consider the Sky Blues the ultimate Midlands club.

But the top-flight’s six London clubs all sit in the bottom eight of the league in terms of average away travel distance, with Palace travelling the furthest (227km) and Spurs the least far (202km). And the very fact that those sides account for just over a quarter of the division means short trips are a regular occurrence.

And for Arsenal, this 11-match stretch that sees them go no further than Brentford could not fall at a better time than the notoriously hectic festive period – certainly when it comes to maximising recovery time between fixtures, which come thick and fast an average of one game every 4.2 days between now and January 5 (though it’s worth noting that turnaround is still below the UEFA-recommended minimum window of five days between matches).

Could the timing of Arsenal’s London residency, so to speak, prove crucial to another successful Premier League title push? Well, they’re already six points clear at the top and look like they could walk it, given Manchester City’s dramatic recent drop-off, but minimising time spent on the road during one of the busiest stages of the campaign seems unlikely to work to their detriment.

That being said, a quick word on Chelsea: the Blues have left London three times all season but are languishing in mid-table in the Premier League and are out of the Carabao Cup. So, maybe there’s something to be said for getting out of town on a more regular basis. Besides, it’s not like elite-level players these days are travelling in anything less than luxury, is it?

Tom Hancock started freelancing for FourFourTwo in April 2019 and has also written for the Premier League and Opta Analyst, among others. He supports Wycombe Wanderers and has a soft spot for Wealdstone. A self-confessed statto, he has been known to watch football with a spreadsheet (or several) open...

#849. Hosting World Cup means decade of excitement - Weir

Caroline Weir says it is "amazing" that Scotland will host the World Cup finals

Scotland captain Caroline Weir says hosting the 2035 Women's World Cup along with England, Northern Ireland and Wales will usher in "an amazing decade of excitement" for the game in her homeland.

World governing body Fifa confirmed on Monday that the United Kingdom will host a football World Cup for the first time since England won the men's tournament on home soil in 1966.

Scotland's national stadium at Hampden Park in Glasgow and Hibernian's Easter Road Stadium in Leith are among 19 venues chosen for the 39-day competition involving 48 teams.

At the age of 31 now, Weir would have to show unusual longevity to still be playing at that point, but she still considers it "amazing news, not just for young players that hope to play there but for us, in this period in between, to develop the women's game in Scotland - and to push it.

"So I think it's amazing news and I think it's going to be an amazing decade of excitement leading into this World Cup".

Andreatta's masterplan to shock Sweden & take Scots to World Cup

Big wins as Celtic, Rangers, City & Hearts progress

The Lyon midfielder has already played for Scotland the only time they have so far qualified for a World Cup finals - in 2019.

"As a young, aspiring footballer watching football on TV growing up, for your home country to actually host a tournament itself, and the World Cup itself, the biggest tournament in football, is the most amazing thing," Weir said.

"So, if I was a 10 or 11 year old girl now, I would be thinking this is the best news ever and I'm going to work and practice and hope that, one day, I am representing Scotland in a home nations tournament playing at Hampden Park in a World Cup for Scotland.

"I don't think it gets any bigger or better than that."

Angie Hind, Scotland Under-23 head coach and Scottish FA player pathway manager, also thinks it will prove inspirational to the young players under her charge.

"If you think of the young players who are involved in our pathway right now, from 13 years old right through the 23s that I take, that's the future," the former Scotland midfielder told BBC Scotland.

"That's very much those players who will be pulling on a Scotland jersey when we are part of that World Cup."

Hind pointed out that it "fits perfectly" with Project 2035, announced this month by SFA and Scottish government, designed to boost the long-term growth of the girls and women's game.

For SFA head of women's and girls football Shirley Martin, it is a "tremendous milestone" considering holding a World Cup had been such "a game changer" for previous hosts.

"Ten years ago, a home World Cup have felt like a dream and now it's happening," she told BBC Radio 5 live. "I think it shows how far women's football has come."

Martin pointed out that the SFA hopes to "double our participation over that time" as well as improving coaching, referees, clubs and facilities - and are already doing so.

However, she admitted: "The one thing we need to do is increase the crowds that come to matches."

#848. Sheehan to miss Ireland's Nations Championship finale after two-game ban

Dan Sheehan has been suspended following a 'croc-roll' on Springbok loose forward Marco van Staden in the Nations Championship; he will miss Friday's fifth-place play-off against Australia

Ireland captain Dan Sheehan will miss Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off against Australia after being handed a two-game ban for his red card against South Africa.

The forward was initially shown a yellow card by referee Christophe Ridley for a croc roll on Springbok replacement Marco van Staden in the 72nd minute of his country's 20-17 victory in Dublin.

The offence was subsequently upgraded to a red card by the foul play review officer.

World Rugby law 9.20d states "a player may remove the jackler from the tackle area by pushing/driving them backwards (including by grabbing the knee/leg), but must not roll, pull or twist an opponent".

Sheehan faced a disciplinary hearing on Monday evening where the panel ruled the incident was a "low entry point" offence and merited a two-week suspension.

The 28-year-old has accepted the sanction and will also miss Leinster's United Rugby Championship meeting with the Ospreys on Friday, December 4.

Typically a hooker, Sheehan started at number eight for the first time at Test level against the world champions.With Caelan Doris, Jack Conan and Sean Jansen all injured, head coach Andy Farrell now faces another reshuffle at the base of the scrum for the meeting with the Wallabies at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

Ronan Kelleher and Tom Stewart are set to continue as the two hookers in Ireland's matchday 23.

#847. What to know about the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship

As ice hockey's governing body continues to wrangle over how to respond to a CAS order to reinstate Russia to international play, the top women's tournament gets underway in Denmark without Russia.

Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time.

The idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

"This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating."

Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception.

Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees powerhouses the US and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.

Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria

Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark

No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.

As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament — and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada with five, USA with three) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February.

Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a world championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milan.

The United States and Canada will play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute.

The Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.

"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice," Hockey Canada said.

#844. Who did figure 3? Why scientists should make experimental contributions visible

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Tito Calì is a Professor of Biochemistry at the University of Padova in Padova, Italy.

Highlighting who was responsible for each experiment could be a boost to many researchers’ careers.Credit: miniseries/Getty

I ask this question surprisingly often when reading the literature. I might be interested in a particular imaging approach, trying to understand an experiment in detail when reviewing a manuscript or simply want to contact a study author who has experience with a technique. I look at the author list, then the contribution statement, and reach the same conclusion: I have no idea who did the work.

After years of working in experimental cell biology, collaborating with other laboratories, reviewing papers and handling manuscripts as an editor, I have come to recognize that this is more than an inconvenience. By obscuring who does what in a research project, we are losing an important piece of information about how science is done — and the people who do it.

Digital badges aim to clear up politics of authorship

Digital badges aim to clear up politics of authorship

This has become particularly obvious to me as my research has become more collaborative. My projects can involve advanced microscopy, molecular biology, animal experiments and computational analysis, each performed by a different group. This is one of the things I enjoy most about modern science: collaborations allow us to answer questions that none of us could address alone. But they also make individual expertise increasingly difficult to see.

When I started in research 20 years ago, papers generally had fewer authors and the experimental work was performed in one or two laboratories. Today, papers routinely have 10, 20 or more authors, with projects spread across several institutes. A 2024 study1 in Scientometrics found that the mean number of authors on papers in the PubMed database grew by more than 50% between 2000 and 2020 (from 3.99 to 6.25). Author-contribution statements help to delineate individual roles in a project, but only to a point. If five people are listed under investigation, three under methodology and four under analysis, I still cannot tell who performed any one experiment.

Anyone who has spent time at the bench knows that experiments require more than simply following the methods section of a paper.

I have seen young researchers spend months, sometimes years, developing expertise in a technique. When the resulting study is published through a large collaboration, that researcher might become one name among many, credited with investigation or methodology. But those words do not tell the person reading the paper that this is the scientist who knows how this experiment works.

For early-career researchers, that’s a missed opportunity. Publications are not only records of scientific findings, they also demonstrate technical proficiency. Being able to say, “I am an author on this paper”, is valuable. Being identifiable as the person who generated a particular piece of evidence provides a different and, in some circumstances, more useful form of recognition.

And there’s another benefit. As a reviewer and editor, I sometimes have technical questions. The corresponding author is, appropriately, my point of contact. But they might not be the person who performed or directly supervised the experiment I care about and, over time, they might not remember who did. PhD students graduate, postdocs change institutions and collaborations evolve. Five years after publication, identifying the person who remembers exactly how an experiment was performed can be difficult.

We rightly devote enormous attention to reproducibility. We record catalogue numbers for antibodies, identify instruments and software versions and deposit raw data sets. Yet we often fail to record something much simpler: who generated the data. I am not suggesting this as a way of assigning blame when something goes wrong — authorship implies collective responsibility for a published study. I see it instead as a strategy to provide traceability of expertise.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03542-w

This is an article from the Nature Careers Community, a place for Nature readers to share their professional experiences and advice. Guest posts are encouraged.

Jakab, M., Kittl, E. & Kiesslich, T. Scientometrics 129, 1299–1328 (2024).

#843. SFA leads tributes to former president Peat

Former Scottish FA president George Peat has died at the age of 86.

The former Airdrieonians and Stenhousemuir director spent four years in the role, taking over from John McBeth in 2007.

He oversaw the appointments of Scotland managers George Burley and Craig Levein and commissioned former first minister Henry McLeish to conduct a review of Scottish football.

Peat was also at the helm when Scottish referees opted to take strike action in November 2010.

"George loved his football and was renowned as a forthright personality and formidable negotiator but behind that imposing exterior lay a sharp wit and a glint in his eye," said current SFA president Mike Mulraney.

"He cared deeply about the national game and his beloved Airdrieonians.

"George was also passionate about the modernisation of the association and commissioned the McLeish Review of Scottish football as one of his first acts as president.

"He was a regular visitor to Hampden, even as his health deteriorated, and will be sadly missed by his friends and former colleagues at the Scottish FA and across the game."

#842. What has happened to Senne Lammens this season?
