#810. How Premier League's big six keep getting richer

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.

We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was Â£120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to Â£442m.

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."

Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.

It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or Â£713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned Â£37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool Â£35.5m and Chelsea Â£33.3m. Newcastle received only Â£13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Their value pillar is projected to be worth Â£25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.

Not just by a small amount. They were Â£74m behind Tottenham, and Â£200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.

City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.

City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.

The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of Â£80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only Â£16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by Â£69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by Â£85m.

"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."

Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.

"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."

The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."

Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent Â£3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the Â£3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under Â£100m."

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than Â£40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are Â£60m and Â£70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.

The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending Â£945m on players in the past five years.

The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

#809. AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

As the news spread from one mathematician to the next, panic set in. On 6 October, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, released more than 700 preprints written by AI, claiming to have solved more than 300 major open problems in mathematics. Some researchers stayed up all night combing through the papers that the company had posted, anxious to know whether their entire research programmes had been rendered obsolete overnight.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Depending on who you ask, this was either the most progress or the most catastrophic development ever to happen in one day in the history of the field — or both. Either way, mathematicians realized that their profession would never be the same. “It’s probably the end of mathematics as we know it,” theoretical physicist Miranda Cheng said at an emergency meeting on mathematics and AI at the Royal Society in London in late October. Many of the papers cracked problems by combining ideas from disparate parts of the discipline, leveraging a universality of knowledge that no human could ever match — and leaving even some of the world’s smartest people feeling completely outdone.

Since then, one of the field’s greatest outstanding challenges, the Riemann hypothesis, also appears to have been solved with AI assistance. And mathematicians across the world have joined frantic collective efforts to confront challenges raised by AI’s advances, from how to evaluate and publish research papers to how to raise future generations of mathematicians. Some see the risk as existential. If mathematical problem-solving becomes mainly a machine endeavour — seen as a utility like water or electricity — then their profession could lose its status in society and human expertise might start to dwindle.

“It’s a challenge like we’ve never faced in mathematics — or in academia as a whole,” says Simon Machado, a mathematician at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) in Zurich.

The bombshell paper drop in October came on the heels of earlier shocks to the field. OpenAI, which is based in San Francisco, California, released a batch of ten important results in August and, in early September, followed up with a historic solution to the Navier–Stokes problem about how fluids flow. The firm had been making noises to indicate that much more was to come. Still, many researchers were surprised by the enormity of the 6 October release. “To just see it as a giant list, without the care and thought and the love that goes into doing this work on a normal basis, it was really jarring,” says Catherine Cossaboom, a master’s student in mathematics at the University of Oxford, UK.

OpenAI posts 700 maths preprints online: mathematicians are up in arms

OpenAI posts 700 maths preprints online: mathematicians are up in arms

Perhaps no source has documented the moment better than Proofs and Prompts, an online forum that publishes essays on the impact of AI on mathematics. An 8 October post titled “100+ reactions to 100+ solutions” collected immediate reactions from dozens of students and career researchers to OpenAI’s 6 October drop. Some wrote poems, others quoted the writers Leo Tolstoy and Stanisław Lem, still others posted fragments from the Gospels (in the original Greek). One contribution reinterpreted the lyrics of ‘Jolene’ by the late country singer Dolly Parton:

And I can easily understand / How you could easily take my math / But you don’t know what it means to me, AI

The tone ranged from the enthusiastic to the angry and the despondent. “Some of them made me really feel heartbroken,” says Albane Théry, an applied mathematician at the University of Warwick in Coventry, UK, who is one of the volunteer moderators of the forum.

Few subfields of mathematics were spared and some were thoroughly ravaged. “Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career was left untouched,” Fields Medal winner Hugo Duminil-Copin wrote to Proofs and Prompts. “I expected that one day we would be surpassed, and that it would happen systematically. But yesterday’s announcement hit with a force I had not anticipated.”

Hugo Duminil-Copin fears that AI will eclipse human understanding of mathematics.Credit: Chris Peus

Duminil-Copin, who is at the University of Geneva in Switzerland, specializes in the theory of transitions in complex systems — such as those that determine how information or infection filters through social networks or how metals can acquire magnetization. (OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, also in San Francisco, had already claimed to have solved a major result in this field in late August.)

Another field that bore a massive impact was the theory of groups — some of the most ubiquitous structures across mathematics, physics and other disciplines. For example, the possible ways of shuffling a deck of cards — and what happens when you revert a shuffle or combine several together — constitute a group, as do the infinite possible ways of rotating a solid object in 3D.

OpenAI’s August batch already contained the solution to a key problem on groups. Soon after its release, during a YouTube interview, Francesco Fournier-Facio, a group theorist at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, UK, mentioned two other problems that mathematicians could now attack with the help of AI. Within days, he was emailed by a PhD student in computational biology who had used OpenAI’s large language model (LLM) GPT 5.6 Sol to solve one of those problems.

Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world

Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world

Fournier-Facio says that OpenAI’s October dump was even more impactful for him personally. It included the solution to a problem on which he had been actively working, called the Boone–Higman conjecture. Overall, OpenAI released solutions to perhaps eight of the top ten problems that Fournier-Facio had dreamed of solving during his career, he told Nature.

But the most stunning AI result relates to what many researchers see as the most important open problem in all of mathematics. The Riemann hypothesis, a question that was posed in the mid-nineteenth century by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, centres on whether prime numbers are scattered across the set of all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as unpredictable as it could be.

AI assistance seems to have cracked it. First, OpenAI proved a partial result, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, in its October dump. Then, on 20 November, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that he had found a proof of the full Riemann hypothesis, working with Claude, the firm’s AI assistant. However, that was quickly followed by a non-AI assisted proof by Rome-based mathematician Alessandro Masullo, which he had been working on for years. “If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” says number theorist James Maynard, a Fields Medal winner at the University of Oxford.

Maynard and many other researchers are excited by AI technology. It is “quite likely to unleash a golden age of mathematical discovery”, he said at the meeting. Another mathematician, Antoine Tilloy at the Mines Paris engineering school, part of PSL University, uses the metaphor that doing mathematics with AI is like riding a dragon: the researcher is still in charge, but the dragon gives them supernatural powers.

‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption

‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption

But the speed at which AI proofs are emerging has already produced an immediate negative reaction. For one, mathematicians, who have long prided themselves on their field’s culture of openness, are now wary of discussing their work in public. “People are even scared to put out an abstract for a talk they are about to give on ongoing work,” says Jakub Dobrowolski, a PhD candidate at Queen Mary University of London. “Nobody wants to share new ideas because of the speed at which somebody else can take them and write a paper,” says Peter Sarnak, a number theorist at Princeton University in New Jersey.

And although established researchers say that they are both thrilled and anxious about reinventing their discipline with AI, younger generations are much more fearful. As Maynard and other established mathematicians acknowledge, the technology already poses severe problems in relation to how to assess merit when peer-reviewing mathematics work that might have been done mostly with AI, and how to train and educate the next generation of mathematicians.

“How do we train people if a good PhD thesis can be prompted out of an LLM? The response from people who are in permanent positions tends to be ‘We’re going to see and discuss’,” says Théry. “But the timescale for that could be too long for postdoc or PhD candidates who will be out of a job in nine months.”

Many early-career researchers told Nature that this uncertainty is their main source of anxiety right now. “While it is clear that faculty are working hard to find long-term solutions to the problems we are all facing, there doesn’t seem to be as much guidance on what to do in the meantime,” says Jad Hamdan, a postdoc mathematician at the University of Oxford. AI poses “more danger the younger you are, and the less experienced you are”, adds Dobrowolski. The toughest problem could be working out how to write a proposal for a research programme that might span two or three years, or more, Dobrowolski says. “Is it realistic? Now I feel like whatever I propose might just expire within a year.”

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

A UK survey of graduate students and academic mathematicians last month by the Martingale Foundation in London found that PhD students in particular are much less optimistic about AI’s impact than are established researchers. Asked if AI would “weaken their development as mathematicians”, 89% of students agreed, compared with only 68% of academics.

#808. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.

European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.

Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.

Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

First, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

With uncertainty over how much support Tashima will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

#807. One of football's most-hyped 16-year-olds - what next for JJ Gabriel?

JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season

It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.

Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.

Before even playing a senior game - barring friendlies - he has told Spanish newspaper Marca his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - with Cypriot and Irish lineage - but he changed his name, reportedly for commercial purposes.

His father, London-born Joe O'Cearuill, played twice for the Republic of Ireland - but the highest level he played at club level was a loan spell with Brighton in League One and one minute in the Uefa Cup with St Patrick's Athletic. He has been actively involved in his son's career.

Gabriel was scheduled to become Manchester United's youngest ever player in the Carabao Cup against Brighton on 16 September, but had told the club he planned to leave by then.

How long will Gabriel have to wait for a first-team debut now? In the past 10 years Real have only handed two debuts to 17-year-olds and none to a 16-year-old.

When Real boss Jose Mourinho was asked about Gabriel on Friday, he said: "I don't have a feeling [about Gabriel]. I don't have a feeling with players who don't work with me."

In fact, Real have not even announced anything yet - despite Gabriel posting a 50-second video montage on social media saying goodbye to United this week.

Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message

Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market

For a while now Madrid have been getting the best young talents early and turning them into Galacticos before they cost in excess of 100m euros.

Vinicius Junior and Rodrygo came that way, then Endrick - and Gabriel is seen as the next.

It fits the policy run by Jose Angel Sanchez, the director general, and Juni Calafat, head of scouting. It is a long-term bet on one of the most promising young players in the international game.

Barcelona looked at him too, and backed away because the commissions were too high. Madrid believe in the player so much that they were willing to pay whatever it took to get the deal done.

The expectations are very high and the aim is for him to reach the first team. They want him at Castilla - Real's reserve team - but the situation right now does not allow it.

Castilla and Real Madrid C cannot sign players until January, so for the time being he is expected to play for the Juvenil - the under-18s.

Madrid also learned from the Martin Odegaard period that training with the first team while playing for the B side is a bad idea. So the plan is a spell in the B side, and when he is ready, Gabriel jumps straight into the first team.

Where Madrid are less happy is with how things have unfolded. Madrid wanted to set the timing themselves and be discreet, because they do not want problems with Manchester United and do not want to upset anyone. At Real Madrid, nobody is bigger than the club.

The idea was to keep everything quiet until January and announce it then. But with Gabriel already training in Madrid, the secret was never going to last.

"Players are moving to him because his reputation is that he'll get you a move to a bigger club," one Premier League club source told BBC Sport.

Dubai-based Barat does not just consider himself a super-agent, but a "boutique" super-agent.

Born in Iran and raised in London, Barat says he fell into football almost by accident after many years in international business.

After initially working as an intermediary at low-level clubs, he founded Epic Sports in January 2020.

His major football experience before that? The football game Championship Manager.

"I was always trading players," he told ESPN this year. "I was obsessed with every single player around the world."

This was not just about living out a fantasy in the real world. Barat was drawn into the profession because of the vast sums agents can earn in commission.

What makes his agency "boutique"? Unlike the top operations which have a huge number of players on their books, Epic Sports aims to have just 22 - two for each position.

This, Barat argues, ensures there is never any conflict of interest in how he represents his players.

Barat offers bespoke management of a player's career and came to prominence in the summer of 2025 when 15 of his players moved on.

This included Dean Huijsen joining Real Madrid, Nicolas Jackson moving to Bayern Munich and Xavi Simons signing for Tottenham Hotspur. Noni Madueke left Chelsea for Arsenal, and the Gunners signed Piero Hincapie.

This led to Barat being named Golden Boy Best Agent for the second time in three years.

Yet he is largely the figurehead, with agents working on his behalf around Europe. For instance, Epic has three other agents registered with the English Football Association (FA).

Barat, who also brokered Moises Caicedo's move to Chelsea, says he uses social media, and in particular influencer Fabrizio Romano, to amplify stories and agree transfers on his terms.

"Ali Barat redefines the game again," read an Epic Sports press release to announce Jackson's loan move to Bayern. No other agency seems to promote itself in this way.

The largely AI-generated video which announced Gabriel had joined Epic Sports was right on brand.

Gabriel's deal is part of a new venture: Epic Future - and this presents an ethical problem.

"It is about targeting the biggest young players, especially where they're not necessarily on the longest contracts," a Premier League source said. "And move them overseas for cheap fees.

"The original club will get a few 100,000 euros if that, and everyone else will hoover up millions and millions and millions - including his family."

Transferring a player to Europe also opens the door to future sell-on fees for an agent, which is against FA regulations.

It is this new focus on younger players which has started to cause friction at some top clubs.

No club wants to lose players they have spent years developing for nothing, only for an agent to reap the rewards.

Manchester United had to work hard 18 months ago to convince JJ Gabriel and his family that Old Trafford was the right place to further his football education.

The big question is, did they overpromise in doing so?

Sources close to the player eventually felt they were let down and United did not deliver on what was expected.

Certainly around Gabriel's pre-season minutes and presence in the squad for the Champions League opener against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK, which it was felt would be a perfect opportunity for the youngster to make his debut.

By the time the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton came round, there was no faith Gabriel would be brought on. Given United lost 3-2, there is merit in that stance.

The secondary elements are where will Gabriel develop the most?

United's academy is one of the best in England at producing young players, but given his size, will the forward benefit more from being in a less physical environment?

There has been a lot of sniping around his decision to leave United, but his stats are impressive and he is clearly a player of huge potential. United would certainly have wished the situation had not unfolded the way it has.

#806. Rob Lowe Makes Rare Comment About His Sex Tape Scandal

Decades after Rob Lowe's sex tape with a woman and a teenage girl—whom he said he believed was at least 21—was leaked, he reflected on the scandal in his new doc Rob Lowe: The Outsider.

Rob Lowe is looking back at a difficult chapter.

Nearly 40 years after the Parks and Rec actor was at the center of a sex tape scandal involving a then 22-year-old woman and a 16-year-old girl, he shared insight into the devastating toll it took on him.

"I'm not trying to do revisionist history, but we were in an over-21 bar," Lowe recalled in his new Netflix documentary Rob Lowe: The Outsider. "I'm a known film actor, and I had to show my ID to get in. I had no idea that one of the girls was underage."

The St. Elmo's Fire star, then 24—who eventually settled a lawsuit with the teen's family out of court and was not charged with a crime—knew that there was always a possibility that filming his encounter with the women could "get out." (Though the age of consent in Georgia, where the encounter took place, is 16, filming a person under 18 engaging in sexual activity is a federal crime.)

"People would ask me to pay a lot of money to try to keep the tape quiet, and I was unwilling to be blackmailed," he shared before sardonically asking, "Boy, I showed them, didn't I?"

When the video did leak in 1989, one year after it was filmed, Lowe learned he was "leading the news" while attending Cannes Film Festival to announce his 1990 film Bad Influence.

"I was advised by Hollywood's finest to not defend myself, so I didn't because they're the experts," he said of the sex tape's aftermath. "As everything began to explode around me, I just hunkered down. Like I stayed in my house. I didn't leave my house."

Since the scandal coincided with the promotion of his movie—which also starred James Spader and Marcia Cross—Lowe faced a barrage of questions about the incident.

"You'd go promote the movie, and you'd get an entire interview and then they go, 'Let me just, one thing I wanna ask you,'" he explained. "I just kind of soldiered on."

As the West Wing star struggled in the aftermath—which included an ill-fated Oscars opening ceremony performance—it was hosting Saturday Night Live in 1990 that ultimately changed the trajectory of his life. Now, he was laughing with the public, rather than just being laughed at.

"Whenever a public figure gets in trouble, Lorne Michaels comes a-callin,'" he explained. "They called me right after the video broke and wanted me to come on and do a bit. I said, 'Call me back when you want me to host.'"

And soon, Lowe found himself at Rockefeller Center's famed Studio 8H alongside the likes of Mike Myers, Dana Carvey and Nora Dunn.

"I was willing to stand in the fire and take my slings for a good laugh, and it wasn't meant as a rehabilitation," he clarified. "To me, it was really, I got a chance to host Saturday Night Live, which is something I'd been wanting to do forever."

Though Lowe—who shares sons Matthew Lowe, 33, and John Owen Lowe, 31, with wife Sheryl Berkoff—has expressed immense regret about the sex tape over the years, he previously revealed that the incident helped him reprioritize his life.

"It's not a great recipe for success to give an 18-year-old male fame, money, drugs," the actor—who got sober in 1990 after a years-long struggle with alcohol and cocaine—said on SiriusXM in 2019, "and expect there not to be something that goes wrong."

"It got me sober, sober got me married," he added. "I've been married 29 years and I have two great sons. I don't think any of that happens without going through that scandal."

For a closer look at more celebrities who've shared insight into their own sobriety journeys, keep reading.

After the two-time NBA champ was arrested and charged with a DUI in January 2026, he became informed on how to fight against his addictions.

“If you do your education, addiction [is where] you suffer from a brain disease, just like cancer or any other disease," he said during an appearance on Page Six Radio that April. "I don't think anyone would wish to have cancer.”

Lamar added, “So, me being educated on disease, the more and more I get educated, the more and more it's easier for me to stay sober.”

The basketball star—who survived a near-fatal drug overdose in 2015—had previously detailed the inspiration he hopes to be to others after passing 60 days of being "completely sober."

“I have a certain type of mental and physical endurance, but when it comes to getting high and escaping, I'm just like everyone else,” he told USA Today in March 2026. “If I could just help the average person and give them faith and hope that they can overcome it, then that's probably one of the reasons why the Lord spared me.”

In October 2018, the American Pie star announced he was one year sober in a celebratory and encouraging Instagram post.

“I first tried to get sober over 5 years ago, when the weight of my obsession with booze and drugs became too heavy for me to handle,” he wrote at the time. “Turns out this s--t is hard.”

He continued, “After some fits and starts, I’ve managed to put together one year of sobriety. I’m as proud of it as anything in my life. If you’re struggling, know there’s help. Don’t be ashamed. We can do this.”

Years later, he reflected on his journey with addiction and the lengths he went to hide the his struggle.

“I’m going to therapy and ‘working on things’ but meanwhile I’m leaving therapy, having just had a good session, and I’m going to the liquor store and buying a fifth of vodka, drinking it and then driving home,” he said on a March 2024 episode of his wife Jenny Mollen's All the Fails podcast. “I knew how to get wasted enough to where I took myself out of the life equation, took myself out of the present, didn’t have to connect in a way that made me feel things.”

He added, “I had it figured out to a T. To not get too drunk where I couldn’t have a conversation with you. I was replacing those bottles in the bar all the time.”

The two-time FIFA Women's World Cup champ has been open about her misuse of Adderall while battling injuries during her college soccer career.

“I was getting really heavily addicted to Adderall and misusing it,” she said on a 2025 episode of the Question Everything with Danielle Robay podcast. “I was taking it all the time. I would go days without sleeping. It was wild. I felt like I was gonna give myself a heart attack. I was crushing it. I was snorting it. It was so problematic.”

However, in the midst of her struggle, her college coach Anson Dorrance was there to support her.

“It got really, really dark and I had to make some serious adjustments,” she explained, “and Anson would have me read books. I started reading this book called [Man’s Search] for Meaning and it's about suffering and reframing it and it changed my life.”

In October 2025, the Migos member shared he was four years sober from codeine—an opioid used to make the soda-based drink sizzurp—after a "wake-up call" from his teenage son Jordan.

"My oldest son kept asking for like pineapple Fanta, but he don't even really drink soda," Offset recounted on Baby, This Is Keke Palmer. "And then one day he came in studio like, ‘Why yours is different color than mine?’ It killed me."

Explaining how the innocuous remark "touched" a nerve, Offset continued, "When I went in my room, I damn near cried."

"I felt bad as a father," the rapper added. "He don't even notice it’s drugs in here though. He don't know, but in my head it's like, him even just saying he want the same soda I want. It's just like, ‘Oh no, I'm influencing him.'"

Over the years, the two-time Oscar winner has spoken candidly about December 29, 1975: the day he got sober.

“I was drunk and driving my car here in California in a blackout,” he revealed in October 2025 on the New York Times podcast The Interview podcast, “no clue where I was going, when I realized that I could have killed somebody—or myself, which I didn’t care about—and I realized that I was an alcoholic.”

After reaching out to a friend for help, he was able to begin a new path. And in December 2025, he reached 50 years of sobriety, doing so with a message to those in a similar position he found himself in a half century ago.

“Choose life instead of the opposite,” he said in an Instagram message. “Life life life and more life.”

The Valley star shared his decades-long battle with drugs in March 2025 after going to rehab.

"I am coming out that I'm an addict," Jax shared during the March 4 episode of Bravo's Hot Mic podcast. "I have substance issues, primarily with cocaine. It’s hard to say out loud."

"I’ve been dealing with this on and off since I was 23 and now I’m 45," he continued. "There was times where I would stop doing it but then there were times where I’d go heavy on it.”

Jax also gave up drinking, explaining, "I don’t necessarily think I have an alcohol problem, but the two go hand in hand. I can’t do cocaine without drinking. So, I just gave up both. I’m proud to say I’m 82, 83 days sober right now, which is the longest I’ve ever gone in my life without either.”

The Spider-Man: No Way Home star stopped drinking alcohol in 2022 after feeling "enslaved" to the drink. "I was definitely addicted to alcohol, not shying away from that at all," Holland recalled on the On Purpose with Jay Shetty podcast. "I think that anyone that has a beer everyday has probably got a little bit of a problem."

"And then you would just reach that moment where you're like 'Wow, I shouldn't have had that last beer,'" the actor continued. "And you wake up the next day and you have a terrible headache."

Since making the lifestyle change, Holland noticed he "could sleep better" and "handle problems better."

"Things that would go wrong on set that would normally set me off, I could take in my stride," he shared. "I had so much such better mental clarity. I felt healthier. I felt fitter."

The star of Hunt for Red October does not often speak to his sobriety journey, which began almost forty years ago.

"I don't discuss this a lot," he said during a May 2024 podcast appearance. "I discuss it every now and then when it makes sense. I'm 39 years sober. I got sober Feb. 23, 1985."

Speaking about his life after moving from New York City to Los Angeles in 1983, Alec explained, "I had a white-hot problem every day for two years. I think I snorted a line of cocaine from here to Saturn. We took it back home. I mean, cocaine was like coffee back then. Everybody was doing it all day long."

And after quitting the drug, he soon turned to alcohol—only to also quit that dependency.

"New York relaxes me," he shared of his home. "I walk around and I see aspects of it that I've never seen before. I'll look at a building and I'll go, 'My God, I never noticed that about that building, those doors.' I have lunches and coffee and my friends."

The Princess Diaries alum shared in April 2024 that she is more than five years sober. As she told the New York Times, "That feels like a milestone to me."

Her reasoning was clear. "I knew deep down it wasn't for me," she shared. "And it just felt so extreme to have to say, 'But none?' But none. If you're allergic to something or have an anaphylactic reaction to something, you don't argue with it. So I stopped arguing with it."

And she's happy she made that decision. "My personal experience with it is that everything is better," she continued. "For me, it was wallowing fuel. And I don't like to wallow."

While accepting the 2018 Woman of the Year Award by the Peggy Albrecht Friendly House, a residential program for women recovering from substance and alcohol abuse, Moore spoke about the "self-destructive path" that nearly derailed her career.

"I feel like there's a defining moments in our lives that shape who we are and the direction we go and early in my career, I was spiraling down a path of real self-destruction and no matter what successes I had, I just never felt good enough," the star recalled. "I had absolutely no value for myself and this self-destructive path, it very quickly brought me to a real crisis point and it wasn't clear at the time the reason. Maybe it was divine intervention."

Moore, who sought treatment in 2012, thanked two unnamed people she "barely knew" for delivering something of an ultimatum to her to turn her life around. "Unless I was dead, I better show up," she quipped, adding that she was given "a chance to redirect the course of my life before I destroyed everything."

"Clearly they saw more of me than I saw of myself," Moore noted. "And I'm so grateful because without that opportunity, without their believing me, I wouldn't be standing here today."

Cyrus shared in 2022 that she's been in recovery for her Xanax addiction since 2020. "It gave me so much structure in the time that I really needed structure, because I didn't want to just be sitting around and stirring in my brain," she told Rolling Stone. "It gave me hope."

The singer added, "Once I felt that it was possible to silence things out for a second and numb your pain, it was over."

She said her friends at the time "kind of cosigned" her drug use and "it just kind of becomes this dark pit, bottomless pit." But, during the pandemic, Cyrus said she was noticing challenges and felt she wasn't emotionally present. "I was completely nodding off and falling asleep," she recalled. "And unable to keep my head up or keep my eyes open, because I was so far gone."

She eventually sought help and noted that "it took some time to get on my own two feet."

The "Lose Yourself" rapper reflected on his prior prescription pill abuse in his 2025 documentary Stans, noting an overdose and missing his daughter Hailie Jade's birthday party prompted a change.

“I cried because it was like, ‘Oh my god, I missed that,’” he said in the doc. “I kept saying to myself, ‘Do you want to f--king miss this again? Do you want to miss everything? If you can’t do it for yourself, you f--king pussy, at least do it for them.’”

Eventually, channeling his energy back into his music helped the Oscar winner on his sobriety journey.

“It did something. It turned the light on,” he explained. “I realized I’m not embarrassed anymore about [sobriety]. I started treating sobriety like a super power and I took pride in the fact that I was able to quit.”

The Parenthood alum was sober for 16 years before relapsing in 2020 by taking Vicodin after a motorcycle accident.

"For the last eight weeks maybe, I don't really know…I'm on them all day," he said on his Armchair Expert podcast. "And I'm allowed to be on them at some dosage because I have a prescription and then I'm also augmenting that."

"And I hate it," he continued. "And I'm lying to other people. And I know I have to quit. But my tolerance is going up so quickly that I'm now in a situation where I'm taking, you know, eight 30s a day, and I know that's an amount that's going to result in a pretty bad withdrawal. And I start getting really scared, and I'm starting to feel really lonely. And I just have this enormous secret."

In 2018, the Halloween star got very candid about her 10-year addiction to opiates, which began in the late '80s after a minor plastic surgery "for my hereditary puffy eyes." The reslt was a prescription that changed her life. "I had a 10-year run, stealing, conniving," she told People. "No one knew. No one."

When her sister visited her in the summer of 1998 and brought along prescribed painkillers for a rib injury, Curtis said she hit her rock bottom. "I knew she had them in her suitcase in our guest room closet," she told the publication, crying at the memory. "I basically took all her opiates. When she was leaving I knew she would pack her suitcase and find her pills missing. I knew I had to acknowledge to her what I had done, and so I wrote her a note and left it on her suitcase. I came home that day, and she put her arms around me and told me she loved me and she was concerned about me and she was unwilling to watch me kill myself."

She attended her first meeting on Feb. 3, 1999, the same day she revealed her struggle to her filmmaker husband Christopher Guest. "He was incredulous that he'd never noticed," Curtis said, adding that she's been sober ever since.

Barrymore, who previously went to rehab for alcohol and drug addiction, shared in 2021 that she was marking a big milestone in her journey. "I'm just going to say something for the first time in a long time: I have not had a drink of alcohol in two and a half years," she said on CBS Mornings. "And it was something that I realized just did not serve me in my life."

She added, "It's so funny. When we reveal ourselves and our truths and the things we've worked so hard for, it's so liberating and vulnerable all at the same time."

Barrymore later explained to the Los Angeles Times that she doesn't use the "sober" label because she doesn't want people to think she's "some perfect Puritan."

"I kept thinking, ‘I'll master this. I'll figure it out,'" she said in 2023. "And finally, I just realized: ‘You've never mastered this, and you never will.'"

The A Star Is Born actor struggled with a cocaine addiction during the early aughts before friend Will Arnett stepped in and confronted him out about his behavior.

"That was the first time I ever realized I had a problem with drugs and alcohol⁠," Cooper recalled during a 2022 appearance on the Smartless podcast. "I'll just never forget it."

Crediting Arnett as "the reason" he went sober, Cooper added, "He took that risk of having a hard conversation with me that put me on a path of deciding to change my life."

The Fight Club star spent years struggling with alcohol before Cooper helped him get sober. "I got sober because of this guy," he told the audience at the 2020 National Board of Review Annual Awards after Cooper presented him with a trophy. "And every day's been happier ever since."

In September 2023, the Cruel Intentions alum shared on Instagram that this was "the longest I've gone since I was a teen without some kind of nicotine or marijuana in my system (among other things)."

"Feeling thankful for the freedom that comes with breaking addictions and dependency on substance," he added. "Sobriety, clarity, and spiritual connectedness feels real good."

After publicly celebrating six years of sobriety on tour in 2018, the singer stunned fans later that same year with the release of the confessional single "Sober," which revealed that she had relapsed.

"Mama, I'm so sorry I'm not sober anymore / And Daddy please forgive me for the drinks spilled on the floor / To the ones who never left me / We've been down this road before I'm so sorry, I'm not sober anymore," she sang.

A month later, Lovato was hospitalized for a near-fatal overdose.

"I have always been transparent about my journey with addiction," she wrote on Instagram two weeks later. "What I've learned is that this illness is not something that disappears or fades with time. It is something I must continue to overcome and have not done yet...I now need time to heal and focus on my sobriety and road to recovery. The love you have all shown me will never be forgotten and I look forward to the day where I can say I came out on the other side. I will keep fighting."

In 2018, she recalled battling her addictions to sex and alcohol. "My sort of addictions jump. They jump around. When I was younger, I definitely think I had a sex addiction of some kind, yes, that everything could be fixed by sex," she said, before sharing about the time she realized she'd developed a troubling drinking problem.

"I remember reaching a rock bottom that time I was in the house by myself and I had those two bottles of wine and was going for the third bottle," she said. "And I was like, ‘Now hold up. You're in the this house by yourself going onto your third bottle of wine? You might have a problem.'"

"So I went cold turkey. That's the thing about me: I can go cold turkey. I am a binger, and I always have to watch myself and I can just get obsessed with things," she continued. "It's not what you're doing but how you're with it. Why you're doing it. It's the behavior that's attached to it because if you want to have a lot of sex, that's great, but why are you having all that sex? That's what you've got to look at."

The Backstreet Boys member tried drugs for the first time before filming the music video for 2000's "The Call," telling Good Morning America years later that he "was off the walls" during the shoot. He got sober in 2021 following a relapse and saw numerous positive benefits just one year later, including losing 32 pounds in seven months by cutting out alcohol and fast food.

"I'm sticking this one out all the way,” he told People in July 2025. "It's a daily thing. But I have finally done what has been suggested amongst the sober community, and my life has flipped in a positive way."

While AJ acknowledged he is "still learning, still growing," he's now confident in who he is.

"I've discovered new verbiage, such as boundaries, never really had those," he continued. "Now I have those, which is a blessing. AJ is a member of a group. He is a persona, but he doesn't define me as an individual. Alexander James is who I am."

After the sudden death of Mac Miller, the rapper—born Shad Moss—took to Twitter to let his fans know that he'd once struggled with a cough syrup addiction. "To the youth- Stop with these dumb ass drugs," he began his series of tweets. "Im going to let something out. When me and Omarion worked on FACE OFF album. I was high off lean everyday! When yall saw me on BET going off on Torae i was high off lean. My attitude everything changed. My fans started to...Turn on me my family too. I never promoted lean in my songs. The whole time i was on the UCP tour with Chris [Brown] I WAS SIPPING 4's atleast 7 times a day. I was addicted until our show in Cincinnati.. i came off stg and passed out woke up in the hospital i was having withdraws.""I never felt a pain like that ever," Bow Wow continued. "It was summer but i was walking round with 3 hoodies on because i was so cold. I missed the chicago show of that tour baltimore show BECAUSE I WAS F--KING HIGH AND SICK!!!! that s--t is not cool and i was doing it to be cool! Kick that s--t! Be a good son or daughter. Be the best you. Ima start being more vocal. We gotta save the youth from going out early. Parents watch your kids. Explain to them. We want yall to live man. I almost died f--king with syrup.""To this day im affected my stomach will...Never be the same and it hasnt been. DRUG FREE IS THE WAY TO BE! smarten up tighten up out here," he told his fans. "We cant lose no more of you. Not one! I love all yall. The young artist all the kids around the world.. dont follow a trend. Break the cycle. PEACE."

With the dual releases of her fourth studio album No Shame and memoir My Thoughts Exactly, the singer spent much of 2018 getting brutally honest about the height of her addition problems. According to Allen, she was abusing cocaine and drinking to the point of being "parisitically drunk. Ultimately, Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin staged an intervention after she accidentally headbutted Orlando Bloom at Kate Hudson's Halloween party and knocked herself out.

She told The Guardian, "Nothing seemed to reach or satisfy me. I remember waking up one morning in those dark days thinking, ‘Maybe it's time for heroin, because nothing else is working.'"

The Parent Trap actor battled a cocaine addiction throughout the '80s that sent him to rehab in 1990. As he later explained on Today, he grew up in the '60s and '70s when "there was a completely different attitude" towards the drug.

"It was even in some movie budgets. I was basically doing cocaine pretty much on a daily basis during the '80s," he admitted in 2018. "I spent many, many a night screaming at God to 'Please take this away from me and I'll never do it again, cause I've only got an hour before I have to be at work.' Then at 4 o'clock in the afternoon I'd go, 'Oh it's not so bad.'"

"I had what I call a white light experience where I saw myself either dead or losing everything that meant anything to me," he continued. He had to sit down then-fiancée Meg Ryan and explain what was going on. Then, he sought help. "That was the end of the love affair with me and cocaine."

After an incident in Newport Beach where the Olympic swimmer tried to kick in his own hotel room door, Lochte made the decision to seek treatment in 2018. "Ryan has been battling from alcohol addiction for many years and unfortunately it has become a destructive pattern for him," his rep told E! News in a statement. "He has acknowledged that he needs professional assistance to overcome his problem and will be getting help immediately."

"Ryan knows that conquering this disease now is a must for him to avoid making future poor decisions, to be the best husband and father he can be, and if he wants to achieve his goal to return to dominance in the pool in his 5th Olympics in Tokyo in 2020," the statement concluded.

Although the Parenthood alum knows that "one of the things that you're not supposed to do is get sober for somebody else," his relationship with now-wife Melanie Lynskey was a major reason that led him to swearing off alcohol.

"At a point, I knew how amazing she was and I thought she would be incredible for someone who deserved her," he explained during a March 2023 appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show, "and I didn't feel like I was that person. I felt a little bit too crazy."

However, as Ritter noted to E! News, he now sees that sobriety is ultimately a personal choice.

"It was easier for me to say that I'm doing it for her because, at that time, I didn't feel like I was sort of worth much," he recalled of the early days of their relationship. "I didn't care as much about hurting myself as I did about hurting her. So, initially it was easier for me to say, 'I'm doing this for her.' And now, I'm doing it for myself."

The country star has been sober for nearly a decade, but it was a hard-fought road getting there. His addiction to alcohol and pain pills began soon after graduating from high school and didn't abate when his career began to take off. He kept a black leather laptop bag filled with bottles of Jagermeister or vodka "at arm's reach at all times," he told previously revealed to People, adding that throughout the day, "every hour and a half to two hours it'd be time to get two or three good pulls on the bottle. And every three or four hours it's time for a pill or two."

And it had no effect on his success. "It wasn't like I was stumbling around all day," he admitted. "I was fully functioning — I wrote more songs then than I do now. That was the scary part."

In late 2011, he was hospitalized with pancreatitis and was told that if he didn't stop drinking, he wouldn't see his next birthday. "I still put it off and was trying to slow down on my own, like, 'All right I'm only gonna let myself take two pills today. I'm only gonna drink this much of my bottle and make a mark on the bottle,'" he recalled. "And it would work a couple days—and then somebody throws a party."

He eventually sought help, entering rehab on Dec. 18, 2011. "I got to the point where I knew it was something I couldn't do on my own," Gilbert said. "Pissed me off to no end and embarrassed me. I'm a pretty strong-willed person but that was the one thing in my life that I couldn't get to stick."

#805. Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year

Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Meet the SPOTY Men's Footballer of the Year contenders

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.

In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.

The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.

Bellingham was recently joined in the England squad by his brother Jobe

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.

Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.

Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015

Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.

Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.

It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.

Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.

He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.

Mbappe has won eight consecutive league golden boots

Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.

By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.

His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.

Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.

His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.

Rodri scored the goal that won Manchester City the Champions League in 2023

Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.

For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.

At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.

He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

Lamine Yamal was 16 years and 362 days when he scored at the European Championship in 2024
