#782. Norway's ice hockey team says Russia replacing it at World Juniors

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

Jennifer Lawrence responded to speculation that she underwent upper eyelid surgery, stoked by The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, as she promoted her haircare line using her signature humor.

Jennifer Lawrence isn't letting speculation cloud her vision.

The Hunger Games star poked fun at theories that she'd recently undergone an eyelid surgery commonly referred to as an upper bleph, which have gained traction online since her return to the big screen for Sunrise on the Reaping.

Responding to her makeup artist Shayna Gold sharing a special delivery of Lawrence's new haircare line, Mes, the actress wrote on Instagram Stories Nov. 23, "iykyk she's the one who did my bleph."

The 36-year-old's one-liner referred to an upper blepharoplasty, a procedure that reconstructs the upper eyelid area, including the skin, socket and fat surrounding the eyelid. According to the National Institutes of Health, it's one of the most common operations done to the face.

Her comment appeared to shut down fan rumors—which were fueled by Gold's recent post of a photoshoot where she styled Lawrence's makeup—that she had elective plastic surgery to reduce her hooded lids. While the Red Sparrow actress didn't deny receiving the procedure outright, her cheeky response hinted that her new appearance is all thanks to makeup instead.

And when it comes to cosmetic alterations, the Oscar winner has previously divulged her latest beauty upgrades, including her decision to receive breast implants this year.

"They’re new," she told Andy Cohen on WWHL, adding of her cup size, "It’s a full C, I think. It’s the same size that they were."

But the beauty founder is prioritizing the balance between sipping from the fountain of youth and protecting her ability to perform her craft.

"I can’t really get very much done," Lawrence told Vogue in September. "I need to have movement in my face—I get baby Botox, but I can't do a lot. If my skin is going to be a little saggier than I would like, at least it looks dewy and pretty."

As such, Lawrence—mom to two kids with husband of seven years Cooke Maroney—explained she is hesitant to partake in facial fat transfers, though she did name what procedure interested her most.

"I would love to have a buccal fat removal. I can’t because everybody would know, but just know that I want that," she said, noting, "I want to continue to watch and see what happens, but I don’t know about that."

Curious about what stars have said no to a nip and tuck? For more celebrities who have spoken out against plastic surgery, read on...

The Euphoria actress confirmed in December 2025 that she hasn't had a boob job.

As costar Amanda Seyfried told her during Vanity Fair's Lie Detector Test, “There’s been a question on everybody’s minds recently, and I just have to ask, are your boobs real?”

“Yes,” Sydney responded. “I’ve never gotten any work done anywhere.”

She shared in December 2025 that she's never gotten filler.

“As you are going along in your journey, I don’t think that you should overdo it with surgery, filler, Botox,” she told People. “You don’t need to do too much. Take it easy. Less is always better."

Travis Barker and ex Shanna Moakler's daughter has been open about her use of lip fillers but denies having cosmetic surgery.

In February 2024, she shared photos of herself wearing a bikini on Instagram, to which a user commented, "This child has done alot of cosmetic surgery @ a very young age, I hope she doesn't over do it! She looks good now!"

The rapper responded, "I really appreciate the love! I'm natural, besides my lips, accept the fact I'm naturally beautiful."

The Twilight alum told Harper's Bazaar U.K. in 2015 she will "never" get plastic surgery, adding, "I am so freaked out by the idea of doing anything. And maybe that's completely arrogant but I don't want to change anything about myself. I think the women who do are losing their minds. It's vandalism."

The Devil Wears Prada star told Good Housekeeping in 2008. "You have to embrace getting older. Life is precious, and when you've lost a lot of people, you realize each day is a gift."

The "God's Plan" rapper shut down rumors in September 2025 that he had plastic surgery to make his abs more defined, explaining the fan speculation was a result of using a photo editing app.

"I came from the gym, I was sweaty in that pic," he said during an episode of Bobbi Althoff’s Not This Again podcast. "Maybe I heightened the saturation or something on it."

He added, "I think I hit it too hard. They don't look like that."

While Drake noted that people go under the knife "all the time," he isn’t one of them.

"People also say that I got a BBL," he continued, referencing the popular Brazilian Butt Lift procedure. "They call me 'BBL Drizzy.'"

The supermodel opened up about why she's all about embracing her skin at every age.

"This is a 58 year old face without fillers, Botox or surgery in good light with professional gorgeous makeup," she wrote in an August 2023 Instagram caption. "I have chosen not to put anything 'into' my face."

She continued, "Some days, I like it. I feel like my face has gained character even as it's lost its youthful prettiness. And it seems a fair trade off."

The Oscar winner revealed whether or not she's gotten plastic surgery.

"My face is changing," she told Allure in an interview published August 2023, "and I love that my face is changing and aging. People think I had a facelift. They're like, 'What did she do to her face?' I'm like, 'Bitch, I'm just aging! It doesn't mean I got bad plastic surgery. This is just what happens.'"

The Pitch Perfect alum admitted she's never gotten any cosmetic injectables, telling People in 2023, "I've never put a needle in my face. And by the way, most people do it and truly, there's no judgement. But I make my living with my face."

She added, "Basically I'm terrified of f--king it up."

The Magic Mike actress set the record straight on whether or not she's gotten facial injectables. "No Botox!" she put it bluntly on Kelly Ripa's Let's Talk Off Camera podcast.

The "Summertime Sadness" singer denied having a surgical procedure on her nose after a fan referenced her "natural nose."

“Still never even been under the knife or anesthesia in my life for the 15th year in a row!!” Lana wrote on Instagram in September 2025, per a screenshot captured by People. “But if u use filler like [my doctor] used to- to build up the bridge of your nose it looks tall no bump. Takes seven minutes.”

The nonsurgical rhinoplasty Lana referred is “a cosmetic procedure where dermal fillers are used to temporarily change the shape of your nose,” according to the Cleveland Clinic. Though the procedure is less invasive, the results only last up to six months.

In 2021, the supermodel, who rose to fame in the '90s as one of the first, sued Zeltiq Aesthetics, alleging that its CoolScupting fat-reducing procedures that she underwent in 2015 and 2016 left her "permanently disfigured." The parties reached a settlement in the case in 2022.

In January 2021, while pregnant, the model wrote on her Instagram Story in response to fans' questions: "For anyone saying 'you need to stop w/ the lip injections': I've never had lip injections (no judging folks who do—ya'll look great!) but you can't even get injections when you're pregnant!"

Jenny from the Block continues to look like Jenny from the Block. In January 2021, she told an Instagram user, "I have never done Botox or any other injectables or surgery!! Just sayin'."

The Friends actress did have a nose job when she was younger to fix a deviated septum, but has spoke out against Botox and other facial fillers.

"There is also this pressure in Hollywood to be ageless," she told Yahoo! Beauty in 2014. "I think what I have been witness to, is seeing women trying to stay ageless with what they are doing to themselves. I am grateful to learn from their mistakes, because I am not injecting s--t into my face."

"I've probably tried everything. I would be scared to go under the knife, but you know, talk to me when I'm 50. I'll try anything. Except I won't do Botox again, because I looked crazy," the actress told Harper's Bazaar in 2013.

The Charlie's Angels alum told InStyle magazine in 2012, "I say, don't fight the rings on the trunk of a tree. Just keep counting 'em."

"The idea of not looking like myself scares me," she added.

The Love Actually actress told The Telegraph in 2011, "I'm not fiddling about with myself. We're in this awful youth-driven thing now where everybody needs to look 30 at 60."

"Nah. It's not my thing," the Oscar winner told MORE magazine in 2007. "I don't have anything against it for other people. Whatever they want to do, I'm fine with it. For me, it's really a self-image thing. Like, I'd rather have somebody go, "Wow, that girl has a big nose" than 'Wow, that girl has a bad nose job.' I'd rather have a comment about who I am than about something that identifies me as being ashamed of who I am."

In 2011, the pop star told Harper's Bazaar, "I think that promoting insecurity in the form of plastic surgery is infinitely more harmful than an artistic expression related to body modification."

In 2011, the Titanic star told the U.K. newspaper The Telegraph that cosmetic surgery goes against her morals, the way her parents brought her up and what she considers to be "natural beauty."

"I will never give in," she added. "I am an actress, I don't want to freeze the expression of my face."

#778. Villeneuve: Verstappen showed 'race craft' edge over Mercedes pair in Vegas

Max Verstappen withstood pressure from Mercedes' George Russell and Kimi Antonelli on his way to winning a thrilling Las Vegas GP for Red Bull; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live on Sky Sports this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Former Formula 1 world champion Jacques Villeneuve says Max Verstappen's Las Vegas Grand Prix victory showed that Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell will not be able to beat the Red Bull driver in next year's championship unless they have a superior car.

Verstappen retained the lead from pole position at the start but was challenged by Russell and then later Antonelli for almost the entire 50-lap race amid near constant changes of position throughout the field, but the Red Bull driver expertly saw off their best efforts before both made late errors to drop down the order.

Antonelli has already been crowned 2026 world champion after Mercedes' dominance early in the season helped him build a significant advantage, but Verstappen is putting together an ominous finish to the year, with the four-time world champion having won four of the last six races and claimed nine successive podiums.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sky Sports F1 pundit and 1997 F1 world champion Villeneuve said after the race: "It was exciting. People will say there was a battery involved [in all the passes], but it doesn't matter.

"We saw some race craft. Max was above and the two Mercedes drivers were lacking in that respect.

"And what it is telling us is that unless next year Mercedes have a car that's superior, they can't win because there's something missing."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

A combination of factors, most notably the extreme power of the slipstream effect, meant there were more than 350 overtakes during a breathless race at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit.

F1: Jamie Chadwick weighs in on George Russell Max Verstappen feud

F1: Could Charles Leclerc's mistakes 'force' Ferrari number one debate?

Oscar Piastri: McLaren team boss Andrea Stella says he liked driver's fiery radio response to warnings to 'be careful' of Lando Norris

Max Verstappen and George Russell: Has feud reignited at wrong time for Mercedes driver after difficult 2026 F1 season?

F1: What is going on at Ferrari? - 'They are learning NOTHING!'

Max Verstappen victorious in Vegas and questions for Ferrari after collision - The Verdict

The lead changed hands 34 times, but every time Verstappen was overtaken, which on almost every occasion was by a Mercedes, the four-time world champion retook his position within a few corners.

Russell locked up and hit a barrier as he tried to pass Antonelli for second in the closing stages, before the Italian suffered a loss of power at the start of the final lap after incorrectly lifting off the throttle as he was preparing to mount a final challenge to Verstappen.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Villeneuve was also impressed by the drives of seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton and last year's title winner Lando Norris, who took advantage of the Mercedes errors to finish second ahead of his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri.

Hamilton could have also ended up on the podium had it not been for him spinning in a contentious collision with his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.

"You could see that Lewis had good race craft as well as Lando," Villeneuve added.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It was really fun to see. We saw today a race where you don't need pit stops, you don't need tyres that degrade.

"We had a race where drivers could push like qualifying laps all the time and that allowed them to race. It was great fun."

#775. Non-league player injured falling down badger hole

Cav Miley has made 17 appearances since joining Chelmsford in the summer

Footballers may be among the fittest athletes in the world of sport, but they are not immune to bizarre injuries.

Dave Beasant famously severed a tendon in his big toe when he dropped a bottle of salad cream, while Rio Ferdinand strained tendons in his knee by lying in one position on the sofa for too long watching television.

The latest inductee into the strange injury hall of fame is Chelmsford City captain Cav Miley.

The 31-year-old midfielder missed the 2-2 draw with Walton and Hersham in the National League South on Saturday after twisting an ankle in training by falling down a badger hole.

Miley returned for the 1-0 home victory over Maidstone United on Monday, after which manager Mark Cooper shed more light on the incident.

"Everyone is telling me it's gone viral, but I told the truth - he fell down a badger hole," Cooper told the club's YouTube channel.

"I was told at the start it was a fox hole, but then the guy at where we train told me it's a badger hole.

"We need to make sure we fill all of them in before we train now."

Miley joined Chelmsford in the summer after spells in the National League with Southend United and Eastleigh.

#774. Klopp advice and Iraola confidence boosts Wirtz

Wirtz moved from Bayer Leverkusen to Liverpool for Â£116m in 2025

Florian Wirtz says he is enjoying his best form yet at Liverpool and benefiting from Andoni Iraola's confidence and Jurgen Klopp's advice.

Wirtz, 23, scored in Liverpool's 4-0 win over Manchester United on Sunday and has three goals and six assists this season.

The Germany midfielder made the Â£116m move from Bayer Leverkusen in the summer of 2025 and after failing to make his mark in his first campaign in England, is beginning to showcase his quality for Iraola's side.

Speaking in Belgium before Liverpool's Champions League game against Club Brugge, Wirtz said: "I can't really say that I've changed that much.

"I've become a bit better on a physical level and that's the only reason that could explain it."

He also said he has been picking the brains of Germany manager Klopp, the former Liverpool boss, while on international duty.

"He tells me all the time that he loved his time here, the people love him here and tries to give me some advice to get successful over here as he has shown how it is done," Wirtz said.

"He can give me some good advice. It's always small things. More private things.

"But he is speaking good about the club, the region, the people, and that helps to hear someone who has experienced it for a long time."

On the influence of Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot as Liverpool head coach in the summer, Wirtz added: "He is bringing me back in a place where I was maybe two years ago where I played really good football, and I can feel that he gives me the confidence and I'm really happy about that.

"I'm just trying to give him back what he gives me."

Liverpool have nine points from their four Champions League games, having won their first three before losing to Fenerbahce in Istanbul this month.

Cody Gakpo and Ryan Gravenberch are both absent from the travelling squad with injuries, with Iraola confirming that Gakpo will be out for the Merseyside derby this weekend, while adding that it is "difficult to say" for Gravenberch.

#773. Dive into the Details of a New Aquamarine Series With Emma Roberts

The ocean can hear that a new series based on the 2006 movie Aquamarine is headed to Disney Channel and Disney+ with original star Emma Roberts reprising her role. Get all the details.

This news will have you glowing from the inside.

A new series based on the 2006 film Aquamarine is heading to Disney Channel and Disney+, with the movie’s original stars Emma Roberts and Jake McDorman coming on board, Disney confirmed in a press release.

In addition to diving back into their roles of Claire and Raymond, Roberts and McDorman are also suiting up as executive producers on the series.

The TV show will follow Kenzi Richardson’s Coral, who moves to a seaside town, according to the press release, and begins to unravel the truth about her mother’s disappearance. In a twist that’ll really have you flipping out, Cora learns her mother is a mermaid just as her own magical powers begin to surface. Briella Guiza, Theodore Dalton and Annika Reese will also star in the show.

The new series comes 20 years after Aquamarine hit the big screen starring Roberts JoJo and Sara Paxton the titular character. In the movie, Paxton plays a mermaid who washes ashore and promises a wish to best friends Roberts and JoJo if they can help her prove true love does exist—specifically in the form of McDorman’s dreamy lifeguard—so she can avoid an arranged marriage by her merman father.

Roberts first made a splash in June, expressing how thrilled she was to be a part of Disney’s Aquamarine show.

“I’m so excited for the new series,” she told People at the time. “I absolutely cannot wait.”

“I’m so excited to bring Claire back to life as a grownup,” the 35-year-old added. “I remember when I read the pilot, I literally got choked up. I didn’t think I would have such an emotional reaction to it, but I definitely got a little teary-eyed.”

And looking back on it now, the American Horror Story actress could hardly believe that fans are literally giving her compliments all these years later.

“There are certain projects that it just feels like lightning in a bottle,” she said. “It feels really cool that we were all just a bunch of girls in Australia making a movie. And now it seems like it meant a lot to people, which means a lot to us.”

While no date has been announced for the Aquamarine series just yet, keep reading to see what the cast of the original film is up to now.

Then the star of Nickelodeon's hit series Unfabulous, Roberts' turn as Clare was her first starring film role. The same year, she fronted the Nancy Drew movie and went on on to appear in slew of films, including Valentine's Day, Hotel for Dogs and Twelve before landing one of the lead roles in 2011's Scream 4.

And in 2013, she joined Ryan Murphy's TV world when she made her memorable American Horror Story debut as meme-able witch Madison Montgomery in the third installment, Coven. She went on to appear in more seasons of the popular FX anthology series (kissing Kim Kardashian in the latest) and lead Murphy's Fox horror dramedy Scream Queens as Chanel Oberlin, another meme queen. Most recently, Roberts starred in Madame Web.

After seven years in an on-again, off-again romance with her Adult Life and American Horror Story costar Evan Peters, Roberts connected with Garret Hedlund in March 2019. They welcomed their first child, son Rhodes in 2020 and ultimately split in 2022. She wed Cody John in July 2026.

The same year she played the titular mermaid, Paxton also took over the role of teen witch Marnie from Kimberly J. Brown in Disney Channel's Halloweentown franchise.

She went on to appear in horror movies like The Last House on the Left and Shark Night, as well as star in the shortlived CW series The Beautiful Lie: TBL. She's also made appearances on This Is Us, How to Get Away With Murder, Twin Peaks and NBC's Good Girls.

In October 2019, she married her longtime boyfriend Zach Cregger.

After turning down the role of Hannah Montana to focus on her music career, the singer made her acting debut as Hailey in the 2006 movie and also appeared in the family comedy R.V.

#772. Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows

Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

#771. Yoro red card overturned, but refs' chief Webb backs decision

Leny Yoro was sent off for this tackle on Alexander Isak

Manchester United defender Leny Yoro has had the red card shown to him at Anfield overturned by the Football Association - even though referees' chief Howard Webb has backed the decision to send the defender off.

Yoro was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott for bringing down Liverpool forward Alexander Isak just eight minutes into Sunday's match.

Isak had run onto a ball that bounced over Matthijs de Ligt but took a heavy touch that meant the ball was likely to run through to United goalkeeper Senne Lammens even if Yoro had not brought down the Swede.

New United head coach Mauricio Pochettino was furious at a decision he felt had changed the course of the game, which Liverpool won 4-0.

"The ball wasn't in his control," he said. "Isak, when he saw the control wasn't good, it's normal to delay, and stop to the run. In that moment that Yoro came from the back, and you go down.

"But all that we play football; you know that wasn't intentional. That is never a foul."

The FA backed that view, meaning Yoro will be clear to face Brentford in the Premier League at Old Trafford on Saturday.

However, in the latest edition of Mic'd Up on Sky Sports, Webb said Barrott got it right.

"I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball," he said.

'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves?

How on earth can the head of referees say a decision was right, but the FA say it was wrong?

"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable," Webb said. "Certainly not clearly wrong."

Not clearly and obviously wrong for a VAR intervention, but clearly and obviously wrong for the FA to rescind the red card.

You wonder how the general fan is supposed to understand it all.

The FA's appeals process is notoriously difficult to predict, especially on highly borderline situations like Yoro.

A commission features three people, usually former players though sometimes there is a retired official is on the panel.

A simple majority is needed, so a club just needs two people to agree with them.

It's why clubs might appeal against red cards when it seems impossible to win, you just never know.

Such was the split of opinion on Yoro, United always stood a chance of at least getting those key two votes.

And this is the crux of appeals process. An FA commission is just the subjective opinion of three people.

Do the appeal again tomorrow with three different panel members, and United might lose.

This is why Pro Ref don't use the outcome of FA appeals to determine how games are officiated.

Two years ago, Brentford's Christian Norgaard won an appeal against a red card at Everton. That was a split 2:1 vote, but enough to say a decision was wrong.

Pro Ref told its referees not to alter their interpretation based on this vote.

Let's throw in another one. The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.

Earlier this season, Brighton appealed against Pascal Struijk's VAR red card at Sunderland.

An FA commission upheld the appeal, but in contradiction the KMI Panel voted the VAR intervention was correct.

Make it make sense, supporters might ask.

This will forever be the problem with officiating, and indeed any hope of true consistency with VAR.

Was Yoro's red card right or wrong? On which side of the fence will the KMI Panel fall?

Football is just a floating mass of subjectivity. Of referees, of VARs, of panel members and of fans. It just depends whose opinion you ask.

Sporting coach Paulo Fonseca speaks to the media ahead of the Champions League clash with Manchester United

United have travelled to Lisbon for their next Champions League match on Wednesday (20:00 GMT).

The early dismissal of Yoro at Anfield meant Sporting had no chance to assess any changes Pochettino might have made after he replaced Michael Carrick during the international break.

But despite United sitting 19th in the Premier League, Sporting boss refuses to accept United are "fragile".

"I don't following the reasoning," said Fonseca, who was only appointed on 4 November after the Portuguese club bought him out of his contract at Lyon.

"Manchester is a great team," he said. "I don't believe a lot that great teams are fragile. The last game they played in the Champions League, they were trailing 2-0, then won 3-2 against a very difficult opponent in Roma.

"Moreover, when they have a new head coach, with such world-class players, it's extremely unpredictable to see if they will have a good day or bad day."

United have not won in the Premier League since August and have conceded 19 goals in their past six games in all competitions.

Yet, such was the nature of the Liverpool game, Fonseca has had to watch analysis of Pochettino's time in charge of the United States to get an idea of what to expect.

"Eight minutes, red card. It's impossible to make an analysis," he said.

"I tried to see Pochettino with the United States and what kind of solutions he used. There is some information but it is very difficult to predict."

#769. Millwall face partial stadium closure after discriminatory chants

Millwall, who are 16th in the Championship, have average league gates of 19,418 at The Den this season

Millwall have been ordered to play a future Championship match in front of a partially-closed stadium as punishment for fans' discriminatory chants.

The club has also been fined Â£70,000 by an independent regulatory commission, and been told another offence this season will lead to a further partial stadium closure.

The sanctions were imposed for ableist and homophobic chants, heard at a game against Charlton Athletic in January.

"These chants are discriminatory, unacceptable, and will not be tolerated at The Den or anywhere Millwall play," Millwall's managing director Mark Fairbrother said in an open letter to supporters., external

"The club condemns them without reservation. They do not represent this club, and the vast majority of supporters who follow Millwall home and away with passion and pride.

"Incidents like this hurt all of us, but none more so than people who are directly discriminated against by ableist, homophobic or other unacceptable chanting, and we apologise to anybody that was affected, offended or impacted by the chants."

Blocks 19, 20, 47 and 48 of the Dockers Stand - the two-tiered east stand at The Den - will have to be closed for the Championship fixture against Sheffield United on 8 December.

It is the first time a club has been given this level of sanction for discriminatory chanting, with the commission saying "the club's previous disciplinary record was a significant aggravating feature".

The commission pointed to chants relating to race in a 2019 fixture against Everton, religion in a 2023 fixture away at Wigan Athletic, and sexual orientation and disability in a 2025 visit to Crystal Palace, all of which resulted in fines for the club.

"History has shown that combinations of action plans and fines have been wholly ineffective to prevent the club - through its supporters - committing breaches" of Football Association (FA) rules around discriminatory behaviour, the commission added.

The FA had charged Millwall in March for the chanting against Charlton.

The club admitted the charge, and in its submissions suggested the chants were limited to 80 to 100 individuals in the north-eastern corner of the Dockers Stand, in the blocks that will be closed as part of the punishment.

However, based on other evidence, the commission concluded the actual figure involved in the chants was "likely to have been in the hundreds, quite possibly more".

It also found that the club did not make any announcement over the stadium PA system ordering for the discriminatory chanting to stop, nor did it deploy any additional stewards or police to the areas from where the chanting was originating.

"I won't dress this up. This is a serious outcome," Fairbrother said.

"This significant sanction was given because, although this is the first charge relating to a match at The Den for many years, the commission took into account a number of incidents of discriminatory chanting involving our supporters over the past few seasons at away games.

"This is the cumulative cost of that pattern. Most importantly, the current and any future sanctions mean the next incident won't just cost the club money. It will cost supporters their seats.

"Innocent fans will be shut out of their own stadium because of someone else's behaviour, and with future sanctions likely to be tougher, that threat is very real."

#768. Blend public cash and private innovation to unlock drug development

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Victor J. Dzau is a professor of medicine at Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA.

Will Ellaissi is head of product at Switchboard, MD, Atlanta, Georgia, USA.

Emily L. Shambaugh is special assistant and policy adviser at Duke University in Washington DC, USA.

A fresh model of research and development is needed to incentivize manufacturers to go after diseases that aren’t sure bets.Credit: Stanislav Gvozd/Getty

For decades, most countries have followed the same model of biomedical innovation. Basic research is undertaken mostly by universities and academia, and private industry leads the translation of research into health solutions1.

This approach has generated extraordinary drugs and therapies as well as economic success. In 2022, the pharmaceutical sector contributed US$2.3 trillion — or around 1.7% — to global gross domestic product (GDP) and supported 75 million jobs2.

How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

However, market failures have been common. Companies have underinvested in developing therapeutics for common diseases with poorly understood biological mechanisms, such as depression, anxiety and kidney disease, because they consider them too commercially risky or unprofitable to pursue3.

To address this gap, we propose an adapted innovation model based on mission-driven public–private partnerships (PPPs), in which government acts as a leading strategic investor. By bringing together the best scientists in academia and industry and lowering risks in industry development in areas of public need and for diseases with limited understanding, this model would accelerate translation, advance health and increase economic returns.

Here, we outline how it would work. It will require systems to ensure affordable access to drugs and therapies, as well as revenue sharing between public and private partners to guarantee public benefits and to support investments in innovation.

Complex diseases that affect swathes of the population create persistent health and economic burdens. Yet, the current biomedical innovation model has proved limited in addressing evolving health needs. Because private investment is guided by assessments of risk and return, it tends to favour diseases with well-defined biological mechanisms and high commercial potential. Diseases that are biologically complex, varied or associated with uncertain markets remain underexplored.

For example, in 2023, more than 300 million people globally had depression. The condition will cost the global economy an estimated $12 trillion between 2025 and 20504. In the United States in 2024, one in five people reported that they had received a diagnosis of major depressive disorder during their lifetime, resulting in an economic burden of $334 billion annually across health-care, household-related and workforce costs5. Yet, the leading drug class for depression (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) has remained unchanged since the 1970s6.

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care

Other chronic diseases impose similarly large burdens. For example, chronic kidney disease affects around 800 million people worldwide — nearly one in seven — and is projected to become the fifth leading cause of death globally by 2040 if current trends continue7,8. Yet, existing therapies cannot stem its toll on human lives.

Antimicrobial resistance is another example, which is associated with 4.7 million deaths globally each year and could contribute to 10 million deaths annually by 2050. Increased treatment costs for people with resistant infections amount to $1 trillion every year9. The antibiotic development pipeline has been depleted over time as economic factors render companies’ return on investment lower than that for other drug classes9. These factors include insufficient funding for research and challenging business models, given the short duration of antibiotic treatments and the need to reserve successful new antibiotics as drugs of last resort, to be used after all other options have failed.

Bringing a therapy to market from discovery can take 10–15 years and cost anywhere between $880 million and $2.3 billion10,11. The majority (90%) of drug candidates fail after entering clinical studies, clinical trials and drug-approval processes12. And companies won’t invest if they are unsure whether a drug will be profitable.

Consequently, many diseases and conditions have no or few available therapies or only modestly effective options13. What’s needed is a mission-driven strategy to guide scientific capabilities and industry development towards areas of public need by elucidating biological mechanisms and aligning incentives for diseases in which market forces alone are insufficient14.

We propose addressing this misalignment of incentives by reconceptualizing the government’s role in therapeutic advancement through a model of mission-driven PPP. Complementing existing grant-based systems, the model would position the government as a principal investor in select areas of therapeutic development.

The government would thus influence which areas of health and science receive concentrated attention and how successful outcomes are deployed for the public good. Such a model could address specific national needs and global challenges. Here are seven components.

Technicians at work in a pharmaceutical factory.Credit: Getty

Select disease targets. We propose the establishment of a government-appointed independent advisory body or commission tasked with identifying priority disease targets using transparent, evidence-based criteria, including disease burden, economic cost, scientific readiness and demonstrable market failure. Further criteria to gauge and consider public input into the selection process could be implemented to ensure public trust.

Set up collaborations. A national government, acting alone or as part of an international consortium, would assume a leading role in supporting basic research into biological mechanisms. It would do so by bringing together basic scientists from academia and translational experts from industry to reduce risks in translational development. Private industry would contribute expertise in drug development, clinical trials, regulatory strategy, manufacturing and commercialization.

Provide initial investments. The proposed PPP would not replace existing grant-based systems or market-driven innovation; rather, it would act as a complement by targeting disease areas in which market risks and incentives consistently fail to generate sufficient private investment. The approach could yield fresh therapies and reduce the cost of care to society while generating revenue from new products.

Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

Could measuring immune health reshape medical care?

In the United States, we propose a federal investment of one billion dollars annually over ten years, directed to specific disease areas. That is less than 1.8% of total US government spending on biomedical research, which was $54.5 billion in 2024. This would be supplemented by smaller investments of 10–20% of one billion dollars from a consortium of philanthropic foundations and industry partners joining the initiative in response to a request for application. Given the high costs of bringing a new drug to market, a $10-billion total investment should provide the scale and time needed to pursue about three major disease targets10–12.

Feed revenues back in. Public return is a defining feature of the PPP. Existing biomedical funding structures are mainly grant making, with the implication that public benefit will emerge indirectly through the downstream health improvements and economic growth spurred by discovery. By contrast, this PPP framework would directly incorporate public accountability as well as returns.

The government would need to leverage its status as a majority investor to ensure access, fair pricing and affordability. It might require conditions such as agreements to ensure access. Pricing frameworks could incorporate a value-based approach to pricing, in which health insurers offer reimbursements determined by a drug’s value for patients. Affordability conditions, such as reasonable-pricing clauses, would also serve as powerful leverage.

#767. Dead hippo to be honoured on football club tifo

Fiona first rose to fame when she was born premature at Cincinnati Zoo in 2017

Major League Soccer side FC Cincinnati will honour Fiona, a hippo that recently died at the city's zoo, with a tifo display at their match with Nashville SC on Saturday.

Fiona, a social media star since her premature birth at the zoo in 2017, died on Thursday after swallowing a woollen hat that had slipped into her enclosure.

The Ohio side will now raise a banner depicting the nine-year-old semi-aquatic mammal in their post-season MLS Cup encounter with Nashville, who won the Supporters' Shield for being the highest-placed team in the league campaign.

Cincinnati said Fiona was a "beloved hippo who became a symbol of Cincinnati and captured hearts around the world".

The tifo will be produced by fan group The Forge Cincy, who painted the display on Sunday in a garage next to Cincinnati's TQL Stadium.

The club will also make a donation in Fiona's memory for every fan in attendance to the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden.

Fan group The Forge Cincy had previously spent two weeks creating a tifo for their "Hell is Real" October derby match against Ohio rivals Columbus

Removal of hat inside Fiona the hippo was 'impossible', Cincinnati Zoo says

Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo

Cincinnati's Nick Hagglund, who hails from the city and is in his eighth season with the team, previously paid tribute to Fiona after scoring in his side's 3-1 victory over Orlando on the day of her death.

The defender yelled "that's for Fiona", mimicking the ears on top of her head, in a celebration video, external on the club's Instagram.

Later, on his Instagram account, external, Hagglund posted, "This one was for her @fionahippo @cincinnatizoo.

"Cincinnati needed a win on the day after the passing of our beloved hippo, a symbol of hope and resilience for our city, and the lads answered the call."

Cincinnati's tifo is one of a number of tributes paid to the hippo, with Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Tee Higgins wearing a Fiona sweater, external prior to his American football franchise's defeat by the Washington Commanders on Monday.

Meanwhile handlers of the blue hippo balloon at New York's annual Macy's Thanksgiving Parade will wear a purple patch in her honour.

At birth, Fiona weighed 13kg (29lb), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species, and she previously inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

From premature baby to social media star - famed Cincinnati Zoo hippo Fiona dies

Fiona swallowed the woollen hat around 10 days prior to her death, with the item getting into her enclosure by accident after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.

Hippos normally live up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo.

Nashville finished top of the MLS Eastern Conference, 31 points ahead of ninth-placed Cincinnati.

However, having beaten Orlando in a one-off wildcard round, Cincinnati defeated Nashville 1-0 in the opening match of their best-of-three round one series.

Should Cincinnati win on Saturday they will progress to a one-off conference semi-final with either Chicago Fire or Charlotte FC, with a conference final prior to the season-ending MLS Cup final.

#766. Khadijah Haqq's Monthly Income Revealed Amid Divorce From Bobby McCray

Khloe Kardashian's BFF Khadijah Haqq said in court documents pertaining to her ongoing divorce from former NFL star Bobby McCray that her average monthly income for 2026 is $5,241.

Khadijah Haqq isn't keeping her finances to herself.

The reality star—who's appeared alongside BFF Khloe Kardashian and twin sister Malika Haqq on The Kardashians and Keeping Up With the Kardashians over the years—detailed her personal earnings in court documents pertaining to her ongoing divorce with ex Bobby McCray.

In an August filing obtained by E! News, Haqq—who broke up with McCray in 2023 after 13 years of marriage—listed her average monthly income in 2026 as $5,241, with another $437 a month in residuals.

And while she has almost $11,500 in savings, the 43-year-old said in court documents that her earnings are "not sufficient" in paying for household expenses for herself and McCray's three kids Christian, 15, Celine, 12, and Kapri, 5.

According to Haqq's filing, her household's average monthly expenses total to $13,892, which includes $4,512 on rent, $1,900 on groceries and $4,658 on school tuition for her and McCray's two daughters.

The Dash Dolls alum also said that she spends roughly $1,176 a month on debt payments, including outstanding medical costs for the birth of Kapri and a credit card bill with a balance of over $11,000. However, she has yet to make a payment on a $30,000 loan from her sister and an $80,000 loan from a "friend," according to her filing.

Haqq is requesting child and spousal support from her ex, whose monthly income she estimates is around $18,645.

In her filing, she said McCray—who retired from professional football in 2010—receives monthly payments of $11,250 in NFL disability and $2,829 as part of the league's annuity disbursement program. Moreover, she claimed McCray also receives $3,044 per month in social security disability. (McCray most notably suffered a bulging disc in his spine during the 2009 season with the New Orleans Saints.)

Haqq argued in court docs that McCray is "more than capable of meeting his own monthly expenses while simultaneously contributing toward" herself and their kids' expenses.

"These payments are for the benefit of the children," her filing read. "There are currently no orders for spousal support or child support."

E! News has reached out to attorneys for Haqq and McCray for comment but hasn't heard back.

For more of what celebrities have said about their personal earnings, read on.

The Jackass star reflected on the "comical" amount of money he was paid for doing death-defying stunts on the MTV series' first season in 2000.

"When it was all said and done, after taxes, I was paid less than $1,500 for the entire first season of Jackass," the daredevil told Playboy in June 2026. "Before the show came out, my sister kicked me out of the house. I was broke, unemployed, and homeless, and a star on this big MTV show."

Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence was paid $25 million to star in Adam McKay’s ensemble disaster comedy Don’t Look Up. But her costar and fellow Oscar winner Leonardo DiCaprio got $30 million.

“Look, Leo brings in more box office than I do,” Lawrence told Vanity Fair for its’ December 2020/January 2021 issue. “I’m extremely fortunate and happy with my deal. But in other situations, what I have seen—and I’m sure other women in the workforce have seen as well—is that it’s extremely uncomfortable to inquire about equal pay. And if you do question something that appears unequal, you’re told it’s not gender disparity but they can’t tell you what exactly it is.”

Her sanguine attitude was hard-fought: When the disparity between Lawrence’s compensation and that of her male costars for 2013’s American Hustle was revealed in the 2014 Sony email hack, it prompted an industry-wide conversation about the gender pay gap in Hollywood.

"I'm so fortunate to have my job. My problem is not money," Lawrence told the U.K.’s Channel 4 News in 2017. "I wasn't upset that I only got this many millions for a movie. That's ridiculous. I was angry about the unfairness and inequality."

The *NSYNC alum revealed that he and his fellow bandmates JC Chasez, Joey Fatone, Chris Kirkpatrick and Justin Timberlake didn't make much money during their years with the group.

“We had a per diem: $35 a day,” he revealed on The Zach Sang Show in 2026. “Our first check was a $10,000 check after years of No. 1 albums, sellout tours. I don’t know how many millions they made off of merchandise because merchandise was insane.”

“And then they finally gave us a check for $10,000,” he recalled. “You’re like, ‘Oh, thanks.’ We should be grateful for that, been working for free for two, three years now.”

Less comparable to DiCaprio’s salary: The $60,000 “before commissions and taxes” that Jonah Hill was paid for 2013’s The Wolf of Wall Street, while the titular wolf made $10 million.

“They gave me the lowest amount of money possible,” Hill recalled on The Howard Stern Show in 2014. But it was the chance to appear in a Martin Scorsese movie, so the Moneyball alum wanted to get the deal done before anyone could change their mind.

“I would sell my house and give him all my money to work for [Scorsese],” explained Hill, who earned his second Best Supporting Actor nomination for his turn as a squirrelly substance-abusing stockbroker. “This isn't what you make money for. You do 22 Jump Street or you do other things, and you can pay your rent. I would have done anything in the world. I would do it again in a second. This isn't about money. You should do things that you care about."

According to Dylan Sprouse, his residuals from filming The Suite Life of Zack & Cody with twin brother Cole Sprouse is anything but suite.

"The only residual check I've ever received for The Suite Life at all was a crossover episode with Hannah Montana for five cents," the Disney Channel alum shared during a 2026 episode of his Wildmen podcast. "In a time where residuals would have been great, not a single paycheck for being arguably one of the most popular shows on television."

While there's no cash prize for nabbing Dancing With the Stars' mirrorball trophy, “whoever makes it to the finale, you all get paid up until then," Jenna Johnson, who won season 33 with partner Joey Graziadei, shared. "And you do get a nice bonus.”

"If you win," Johnson, who noted pro contracts are dependent on seniority, continued. "it’s not like you get a million dollars. You’re just getting a cute trophy together.” As for those who say farewell to the ballroom early, well, as she explained, "You’re guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks.” According to multiple reports, dancer salaries start at around $1,200 to $1,600 an episode, which can increase to up to of $100,000 per season. (ABC has not confirmed these reports.) On the flip side, celebrities receive a starting salary of $125,000. As they cha-cha further into the competition, stars  receive additional bonuses with the semifinalists and finalists getting paid up to $50,000 extra.

The actress seemingly confirmed that the Friends cast—including Jennifer Aniston, Courtney Cox,David Schwimmer and Matt LeBlanc—get $20 million in residuals per year from the show re-airing, quipping to The Times in April 2026 that if she had to guess why, it's “Because Phoebe Buffay was so great?"

But in actuality, she praised the talents of her costars for their performances.

“I felt I did OK, but Jennifer and Courteney? Amazing,” she raved. “David and Matt? They had me laughing so hard. And then Matthew [Perry]—he was just beyond us all.”

To hear Joe Giudice tell it, his and ex-wife Teresa Giudice's salary for season one of The Real Housewives of New Jersey was nothing to flip over. "We got paid nothing the first season," he detailed on daughter Gia Giudice's Casual Chaos podcast in August 2025. "I'll even say, it was like $25,000. It was ridiculous. But, whatever."

And the ingredientses they put into that initial fame-making season weren't cheap. "I think the first year we had that big party in my great room," the father of four reflected. "I think that show cost me $150,000 the first year."

Oprah Winfrey happily accepted only a little bit of green to star in 1985’s The Color Purple.

“They were only offering $35,000 to be in this film, and it is the best $35,000 I ever earned,” the billionaire media mogul told Essence in 2023. “It changed everything and taught me so much.”

The actress revealed that she made about $20,000 per episode of Two and a Half Men with a 5 percent raise each season, making about $43,000 for one episode in the final season.

When she scored the role of late Tejana singer Selena Quintanilla in the 1997 biopic Selena, Jennifer Lopez became the first Latina actress to earn $1 million for a film.

“I was too young and didn’t know what the hell was going on,” Lopez told Variety in 2019, reflecting on her breakout movie. “It was great they offered me a million dollars. I feel like everyone was making a statement.”

And it paved the way for her to make hundreds of millions more, though sometimes her participation doesn’t cost a thing.

“I do things because I love them,” Lopez explained to GQ in 2019. “I didn't get paid a whole bunch of money for Hustlers. I did it for free and produced it. I bank on myself, you know? Like Jenny From the Block—I do what I love."

Adrien Brody didn’t do The Brutalist for the money. Rather, he took on the role of a Hungarian architect suffering for his art in post-WWII America for $250,000 and won his second Oscar for Best Actor.

“I need a studio movie now, because I’ve poured it all into this,” Brody quipped to Variety, referring to the “barn that looks like a castle” he’s renovating in upstate New York.

“Do you guys know what they pay us?” Pete Davidson cracked to New York magazine when asked ahead of Saturday Night Live's 50th anniversary special how he spent his money when he was first hired at the age of 20 in 2014. “It’s like three grand an episode, so I think I got dinner.”

Interestingly, the salaries have remained proportional for SNL newcomers, with season one stars John Belushi, Jane Curtin, Gilda Radner, Dan Aykroyd and Chevy Chase reportedly earning $750 an episode back in 1975. Which was roughly equivalent to $3,300 in 2014, according to the Consumer Price Index Inflation calculator. (Though the $750 of 1975 is $4,428 in 2025.)

While Kenan Thompson makes a lot more than $3,000 per episode of SNL now that he’s in his record 22nd season, the former Nickelodeon star had to start somewhere.

“That first commercial when they paid me, it was $800,” the All That alum revealed in Demi Lovato‘s 2024 documentary Child Star. “I was 12 so that may as well have been a million dollars."

It turns out Gilmore Girls’ status as a beloved rewatchable classic is literally priceless.

“There really are no residuals on Netflix,” Lauren Graham, who played Lorelai Gilmore for seven seasons and then reprised the role for 2016’s Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life, said on Jimmy Kimmel Live in March 2025. “But I’ve been paid in love and appreciation.”

Feeling not so appreciated, Tommy Dorfman got specific about her 13 Reasons Why paycheck during the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike—which was prompted in part (as was the WGA strike) by streamers like Netflix not making it a practice to pay additional compensation to cast and crew once a show had become a big hit.

"my earnings for the entire first season of 13 reasons why were $29,953.24 prior to agency and manager fees (20%) and taxes," Dorfman wrote on Threads July 24. "8 episodes over six months." She continued, “i did all of the promo and had KEY ART for this show, flew round trip from NYC to SF to shoot for every episode, was kept for days without pay/working. i barely qualified for insurance."

And, Dorfman added, “within the first 28 days of release, the show's season 1 garnered a total of 476 million view hours. this is why we strike."

Without naming names or numbers, Dax Shepard told fellow Parenthood alum Lauren Graham when she appeared on his podcast that he knew he made “among the lowest of all the actors” on their NBC drama, which ran for six seasons.

But, the Armchair Expert host stressed that he did not mind.

“Every job I had ever had in my life prior to Parenthood, I made a point to find out what everyone was making,” he said. “I'd always figure it out—either a conversation where I get it out of them or I backchannel through an agent."

So he made a point to purposely not seek out such info about his Parenthood family, which helped with enjoying the experience even when he did get an inkling of where he was on the pay pyramid.

“I got a dollar for writing the script,” George Clooney told the Los Angeles Times in 2005 about the financial strings he pulled to get his film Good Night, and Good Luck made. “I had to endorse my check for directing and turn in my acting salary. [Actor, cowriter and coproducer Grant Heslov] and I each made a buck for doing it.”

His labor of love about CBS News journalist Edward R. Murrow speaking truth to power in the 1950s had legs, though: Making his Broadway debut, Clooney wrapped his months-long stint playing Murrow in a stage adaptation of the film  in June 2025. And with the play having grossed a Broadway record (for a nonmusical) $3.3 million during a preview week before it officially opened April 3, he made a lot more than $1.

For his chilling turn as Patrick Bateman in 2000’s American Psycho, Christian Bale was paid “the absolute minimum they were legally allowed to pay me” because no one in the production really wanted to hire him except director Mary Harron, the Welsh actor told GQ in 2022.

He made so little, Bale shared, that he remembered “sitting in the makeup trailer and the makeup artists were laughing at me because I was getting paid less than any of them.”

No, the Game of Thrones cast didn't get paid $300,000 per episode, according to Emilia Clarke.

“We didn’t earn that much," she told Variety in 2026. "Can you imagine? I’d have been driving a couple of Porsches!"

However, the actress—who played Daenerys Targaryen for eight seasons between 2011 and 2019—noted that the money she made throughout the HBO show did provide her with enough financial security to pay off her parents’ mortgage.

His uncle may have been Rico, but Jon Heder confirmed in 2010 that he was “initially” only paid $1,000 for Napoleon Dynamite.

After the irreverent comedy became a sleeper hit, he was able to renegotiate for a piece of the profits, telling the New Zealand Herald, “They went a little bit higher.”

Djimon Hounsou said he’s “definitely underpaid” in Hollywood despite his prestigious list of credits, including Amistad and Blood Diamond.

"I've been in this business and making films now over two decades," the Beninese actor told CNN’s Larry Madowo in January 2025. "And still—with two Oscar nominations and been in many big blockbuster films—and yet I’m still struggling financially to make a living."

Rebel Wilson detailed in her 2024 memoir Rebel Rising that she was paid $3,500 to do Bridesmaids, “a fee that I then had to pay directly to the Screen Actors Guild to join the union. So really, I got paid nothing.”

Still, she wrote, the experience was “everything!”

And the Australian actress’ star rose ever a-ca higher, with her fee going from the SAG minimum scale of $65,000 for 2012’s Pitch Perfect to $10 million for 2017’s Pitch Perfect 3. Wilson wrote that she raked in $20 million total for the threequel, Isn’t It Romantic and The Hustle, though—reality alert—she “lost almost 50 percent to taxes, 10 percent to agents and 5 percent” to her lawyer. But even after those obligations and paying her publicist, business manager and assistant, Wilson “netted what to me was an absolute fortune.”

In late 2017, Ellen Pompeo negotiated a new Grey’s Anatomy contract for $575,000 per episode, a seven-figure signing bonus and two full backend equity points worth an estimated $6 million to $7 million.

“I’m 48 now, so I’ve finally gotten to the place where I’m OK asking for what I deserve, which is something that comes only with age,” Pompeo told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018. “Because I’m not the most ‘relevant’ actress out there. I know that’s the industry perception because I’ve been this character for 14 years. But the truth is, anybody can be good on a show season one and two. Can you be good 14 years later? Now, that’s a f--kin’ skill.”

Reflecting more recently on how she always made less than costar Patrick Dempsey, even though she was the Grey in question, Pompeo said she didn’t begrudge him his money.

But, she said on a March 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy, “Just being that I was the namesake of the show, I deserved the same and that was harder to get. I wasn't salty about him getting what he got. I was salty that they didn't value me as much as they valued him and they never will.”

Jamie Lee Curtis recalled getting paid $2,000 a week—so $8,000 in total—for 1978’s Halloween, her movie debut. “I mean,” she told Rotten Tomatoes in 2018, “nobody got paid, anything.”

Yet while the scream queen earned four figures, director John Carpenter’s friend Nick Castle felt like a king making $25 per day to share the role of Michael Myers. (It’s Anthony Moran whose face you see when the killer’s mask comes off for a freaky second, and editor Tommy Lee Wallace also logged screentime as Michael.)

“That was a lot at the time!” Castle, who attended film school at USC with Carpenter, told Vanity Fair in 2018. “You have to remember: My interest in doing the film was being on set, so I could demystify the experience of filmmaking and directing. I expected to hang around the set for no money. But hey, $25 per day, and all I had to do was wear a rubber mask.”

Taraji P. Henson earned a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination for 2008’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, but years later she was still fired up by the $150,000 she accepted to be in the movie—after producers rejected the $500,000 quote she brought to the table.

As for the film’s leads Brad Pitt and Cate Blanchett, “You don’t hear a lot of $20 million quotes anymore, but at this time that was happening,” Henson said on the Ladies First With Laura Brown podcast in 2021. “And rightfully so—I’m not saying they shouldn’t have paid Cate and Brad what they deserved.”

But, she continued, “I’m bringing a certain amount to the seat too and I felt like what I was asking at that time in my career was fair, was fair to the ticket sales that I would contribute to this big film. Wouldn’t do it.” Henson was “gutted” when they offered $100,000, she recalled. “When it was all said and done I got $150,000, but I had to swallow my pride, baby.”

Breaking it down, “I know people go, ‘$150,000, that’s a lot of money!’” Henson acknowledged. “I don’t ever want people to think that I’m ungrateful because that is not me.” But, she calculated, “Uncle Sam is going to take 50 percent of that, so now you’re left with, what? $75,000. Now before Uncle Sam takes the money, I have to pay my team before taxes, 30 percent. So once Uncle Sam takes his 75, then I got another 30 that’s coming off of that 75, so I may have made $40,000?”

While Blanchett has made plenty of money over the years, it didn’t all come from playing royal elf Galadriel in The Lord of the Rings franchise, though it grossed $2.9 billion at the worldwide box office.

“Are you kidding me? No,” she retorted on Watch What Happens Live in August 2024 when Andy Cohen guessed LOTR was her biggest paycheck. “No one got paid anything to do that movie…I mean, I basically got free sandwiches, and I got to keep my ears.”

They weren’t paid a precious amount, that is. Orlando Bloom, who played elven warrior Legolas, shared on The Howard Stern Show in 2023 that he made $175,000 for the whole trilogy.

#765. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.
